title: Potential Hormone–Immune–Viral Interplay in HPV Persistence: From Antiviral Clearance to Neoplastic Progression
abstract: Persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection has been strongly associated with cervical carcinogenesis, yet the factors determining viral clearance versus persistence remain incompletely understood. Endocrine signaling has been proposed as a potential modifier of HPV-associated immune responses, particularly through the 17β-estradiol–estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) axis. This review evaluates evidence linking hormonal signaling with HPV acquisition, viral burden, persistence, clearance, and neoplastic progression, distinguishing these outcomes rather than treating them as interchangeable. Human evidence directly addressing HPV persistence is limited and largely observational, with important constraints related to small sample sizes, contraceptive exposure, heterogeneous hormone measurements, confounding, and the frequent absence of genotype-specific longitudinal follow-up. Experimental papillomavirus models provide stronger evidence that estradiol and ERα can modify viral burden, disease, immune-cell profiles, and clearance-related outcomes, although findings from murine infection models and HPV-transgenic carcinogenesis models cannot be directly extrapolated to persistent HPV infection in women. Evidence for progesterone, prolactin, and glucocorticoid-related pathways is more indirect and derives mainly from ex vivo, cellular, or neoplastic models. Overall, current data support endocrine signaling as a biologically plausible modifier of HPV-associated immunity and disease, but a causal hormone–immune–viral interaction determining genotype-specific persistence has not yet been established. Longitudinal human studies and experimental models with persistence or clearance as predefined endpoints are needed to resolve this question.

title: Understanding Cervical Screening Engagement Among Young South Asian Women: Perspectives of Women and Healthcare Professionals.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite increased uptake of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, cervical screening participation among younger South Asian women has declined, particularly in deprived areas in England. The reasons for this pattern remain poorly understood. This study explored barriers and facilitators to cervical screening among South Asian women aged 25-29 in a deprived locality. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with South Asian women aged 25-29 (n = 15) and healthcare professionals involved in cervical screening delivery (n = 6) in Blackburn with Darwen. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. RESULTS: Barriers to screening were multifactorial and included limited understanding of cervical screening and HPV, cultural norms surrounding modesty and sexuality, fear of community judgement and embarrassment, and structural challenges such as appointment access and competing responsibilities. Family networks acted as both barriers and facilitators. Healthcare professionals described adapting language to reduce fear, but highlighted service pressures related to staffing and funding, which constrained proactive engagement. Although most women reported receiving the HPV vaccination, understanding of HPV and the continued importance of cervical screening remained limited, highlighting opportunities to reinforce cervical screening education. CONCLUSION: Cervical screening engagement among young South Asian women is shaped by intersecting cultural, emotional, and structural influences, which may be intensified in deprived settings. HPV vaccination should be accompanied by clear communication about the continued importance of cervical screening, particularly where knowledge and awareness remain low. Culturally responsive communication, flexible service provision and community partnership approaches are needed to address persistent inequalities in screening uptake. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: The study was informed by prior community engagement and public involvement work with underserved populations. Interview guides were developed in collaboration with a public advisor from the South Asian community to ensure they were relevant, inclusive, and reflective of community priorities.

title_zh: 了解南亚年轻女性的宫颈筛查参与度:女性和医疗保健专业人员的观点。
source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Despite increased uptake of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, cervical screening participation among younger South Asian women has declined, particularly in deprived areas in England. The reasons for this pattern remain poorly understood. This study explored barriers and facilitators to cervical screening among South Asian women aged 25-29 in a deprived locality. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with South Asian women aged 25-29 (n = 15) and healthcare professionals involved in cervical screening delivery (n = 6) in Blackburn with Darwen. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. RESULTS: Barriers to screening were multifactorial and included limited understanding of cervical screening and HPV, cultural norms surrounding modesty and sexuality, fear of community judgement and embarrassment, and structural challenges such as appointment access and competing responsibilities. Family networks acted as both barriers and facilitators. Healthcare professionals described adapting language to reduce fear, but highlighted service pressures related to staffing and funding, which constrained proactive engagement. Although most women reported receiving the HPV vaccination, understanding of HPV and the continued importance of cervical screening remained limited, highlighting opportunities to reinforce cervical screening education. CONCLUSION: Cervical screening engagement among young South Asian women is shaped by intersecting cultural, emotional, and structural influences, which may be intensified in deprived settings. HPV vaccination should be accompanied by clear communication about the continued importance of cervical screening, particularly where knowledge and awareness remain low. Culturally responsive communication, flexible service provision and community partnership approaches are needed to address persistent inequalities in screening uptake. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: The study was informed by prior community engagement and public involvement work with underserved populations. Interview guides were developed in collaboration with a public advisor from the South Asian community to ensure they were relevant, inclusive, and reflective of community priorities.
abstract_zh: 背景:尽管 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 疫苗 的使用率有所增加,但南亚年轻女性的宫颈筛查参与率有所下降,特别是在英格兰的贫困地区。造成这种模式的原因仍然知之甚少。本研究探讨了贫困地区 25-29 岁南亚女性宫颈筛查的障碍和促进因素。方法:与 Darwen 一起对布莱克本 25-29 岁的南亚女性 (n = 15) 和参与宫颈筛查的医疗保健专业人员 (n = 6) 进行半结构化访谈。使用反思性主题分析对数据进行分析。结果:筛查的障碍是多因素的,包括对宫颈筛查和 HPV 的了解有限、关于谦虚和性的文化规范、对社区判断和尴尬的恐惧,以及预约机会和竞争责任等结构性挑战。家庭网络既是障碍又是促进者。医疗保健专业人员描述了调整语言以减少恐惧,但强调了与人员配置和资金相关的服务压力,这限制了积极参与。尽管大多数女性报告接受了 HPV 疫苗接种,但对 HPV 和宫颈筛查的持续重要性的了解仍然有限,这凸显了加强宫颈筛查教育的机会。结论:南亚年轻女性的宫颈筛查参与度受到文化、情感和结构等交叉影响的影响,这种影响在贫困环境中可能会加剧。HPV 疫苗接种 应伴随着关于宫颈筛查的持续重要性的明确沟通,特别是在知识和意识仍然较低的情况下。需要采取文化敏感的沟通、灵活的服务提供和社区伙伴关系方法来解决筛查方面持续存在的不平等问题。患者或公众贡献:该研究是根据先前的社区参与和针对服务不足人群的公众参与工作而进行的。访谈指南是与南亚社区的公共顾问合作制定的,以确保它们具有相关性、包容性并反映社区的优先事项。

title: Photo Controlled CRISPR/Cas12a Microdroplets for Amplification-free Nucleic Acid Detection.
abstract: Microdroplet platforms provide an amplification-free CRISPR diagnostic method by confining reactions to enhance local target concentration, but spontaneous Cas12a cleavage during droplet generation can generate false-positive signals that compromise quantitative accuracy. To address this, LUCID (Light-Up Cas12a In microDroplets), a photoactivatable CRISPR/Cas12a microdroplet platform was developed for amplification-free, digital nucleic acid detection. The strategy employs a photocloaking modification on crRNA that temporarily blocks Cas12a activity. Brief UV irradiation after droplet formation synchronously activates trans-cleavage across all droplets, eliminating premature signal generation. The platform detected HPV16 DNA down to 100 copies/μL and exhibited excellent specificity against non-target sequences. LUCID accurately discriminated genotyped HPV16/18 in multiple cervical cancer cell lines. By uniquely integrating optical controllability, amplification-free operation, and digital readout, LUCID effectively eliminates false positives and enables absolute quantification, offering a versatile and robust platform for diverse nucleic acid detection applications.

title: [HPV vaccination in young men and prevention of penile cancer].
abstract: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is responsible for a substantial proportion of anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers in men. Approximately 30 to 50 % of penile squamous cell carcinomas are associated with high-risk HPV infection. Although HPV vaccination is widely recognized as an effective strategy for cervical cancer prevention, the benefits of vaccinating boys remain less widely understood. Because penile cancer is rare and has long latency period, direct evidence that vaccination reduces its incidence remains limited. However, available data show that HPV vaccination reduces persistent HPV infections, genital warts, and certain HPV-related precancerous lesions in men, supporting an expected long-term benefit in the prevention of HPV-related cancers.

title: Análise epidemiológica da cobertura vacinal contra o HPV e sua relação com a prevenção do câncer do colo do útero no Brasil
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) represents a major public health concern due to its high transmissibility and association with the development of neoplasms, particularly cervical cancer. In this context, vaccination is one of the main prevention strategies, although inequalities in vaccination coverage persist in Brazil. This study aimed to analyze HPV vaccination coverage across Brazil, considering differences between sexes, distribution among states, and implications for cervical cancer prevention. This is an epidemiological, observational, ecological, descriptive, and retrospective study with a quantitative approach, based on secondary data provided by the Brazilian Ministry of Health and the VacinaBR 2025 Yearbook. National indicators for 2022, 2024, and 2025 were analyzed, as well as first-dose vaccination coverage among adolescents who turned 15 years old in 2024, according to the Brazilian states and the Federal District. The results showed an increase in national vaccination coverage between 2022 and 2025, from 78.38% to 86.22% among girls and from 45.43% to 74.55% among boys. Despite this improvement, coverage rates remained below the 90% target. The state-level analysis revealed substantial territorial disparities, with vaccination coverage among boys remaining lower than among girls in all Brazilian states and the Federal District. In Bahia, vaccination coverage indicators for the 2024 cohort reached 86.2% among girls and 57.4% among boys. These findings highlight progress in immunization, but also the persistence of inequalities that hinder the achievement of established targets. It is concluded that strengthening vaccination strategies, combined with health education, active outreach, and epidemiological monitoring, is essential to expand population protection and contribute, in the long term, to cervical cancer prevention in Brazil.

title: Molecular Detection of Opportunistic Bacterial Targets, Antibiotic Resistance Genes and 21 HPV Genotypes in the Urogenital Tract of Mongolian Men: A Hospital-Based Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Molecular data on urogenital opportunistic bacteria, antibiotic resistance genes and human papillomavirus (HPV) genotypes in Mongolian men are scarce. In this cross-sectional study of adult men at an andrology clinic in Ulaanbaatar (2024–2025), quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detected 25 bacterial targets (n = 137), 14 resistance genes (n = 152) and 21 HPV genotypes (n = 117) in urethral swabs. (65.7%), Streptococcus spp. (50.4%) and Enterobacterales (39.4%) predominated, mostly at low loads; only 2.7% of positive results reached an exploratory reference load (≥5 log10 copies/sample; not a validated diagnostic cut-off). mecA was detected in 30.9% and blaTEM in 4.6%; acquired carbapenemase and vanA/vanB genes were not detected. mecA was co-detected with Staphylococcus spp. (odds ratio [OR] 3.43; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.20–9.79), but not after multivariable adjustment (OR 2.59; 0.87–7.68). Among men in whom HPV testing was ordered, HPV was detected in 74.4% (65.8–81.4), high-risk and multiple genotypes in 51.3% each; HPV11 (29.9%), HPV6 (29.1%), HPV16 and HPV51 (16.2% each) predominated. HPV detection decreased with age (OR 0.64 per 5 years; 0.47–0.85), and 90.8% of HPV-positive men carried nine-valent vaccine genotypes. These findings apply to a selected clinic-based sample and are not population prevalence estimates; molecular detection did not distinguish colonisation from infection, and positive PCR results should be interpreted together with load and clinical findings.

title: Effectiveness of A Self-Instructional Module On Knowledge Regarding HPV Vaccine Among Parents of Adolescent Girls Residing in Selected Areas: A Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: Cervical cancer remains an important public health problem, and persistent infection with high-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 16 and 18, is a major cause. Although HPV vaccination provides an important opportunity for primary prevention, parental awareness and misconceptions may influence acceptance and uptake. The present study assessed whether a self-instructional module (SIM) could improve parents’ knowledge regarding HPV vaccination. Objectives The primary objective was to assess the effectiveness of a self-instructional module on knowledge regarding HPV vaccination among parents of adolescent girls residing in selected areas. The secondary objective was to determine the association between post-test knowledge scores and selected demographic variables. Methodology: A quantitative, quasi-experimental one-group pre-test post-test design was adopted. Seventy parents of adolescent girls were selected by non-probability convenience sampling from selected urban, semi-urban and rural areas. Data were collected using a validated self-structured 25-item knowledge questionnaire. The tool was validated by 22 experts and demonstrated reliability of 0.9195 using Karl Pearson’s correlation coefficient. A pre-test was conducted on day 1, followed by administration of the self-instructional module, and the post-test was conducted on day 7. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used for analysis. Results In the pre-test, 80% of parents had poor knowledge and 20% had average knowledge. The mean pre-test knowledge score was 4.92 ± 1.14. After the intervention, 2.86% had good knowledge, 68.57% had very good knowledge and 28.57% had excellent knowledge. The mean post-test score increased to 19.44 ± 2.26. The mean difference was 14.51 ± 1.62 and the paired t-value was 74.77 with 69 degrees of freedom, demonstrating a statistically significant improvement at the 0.05 level. Post-test knowledge was significantly associated with gender, religion, type of family, area of residence, educational status, occupation, monthly family income and previous knowledge of HPV vaccination. No significant association was found with age or source of information. Conclusion : The findings demonstrate that the selfinstructional module was effective in improving parental knowledge regarding HPV vaccination. Structured and accessible educational materials may therefore be useful in community and adolescent health education, particularly where baseline knowledge is limited.

title: Cox-2 mediated oncogenic signaling in head and neck cancer: implications for drug repurposing
abstract: Head and neck cancers (HNC) are a group of heterogeneous tumors with ~90% developing from the squamous lining of the oral cavity, pharynx and larynx. The risk factors include use of tobacco and/or alcohol, human papilloma virus (HPV) infection, poor oral hygiene, improper diet(1) besides other environmental factors. HPV is mainly associated with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSC) which is commonly diagnosed in younger patients without any history of smoking or drinking (1). HPV driven cancers are more responsive to treatment, and patients tend to have a better survival rate compared to other types of HNC. HNC is characterized by its aggressive nature, tendency for local invasion and metastasis which explains its poor prognosis (2).The survival outcomes of HNC depends on certain prognostic factors such as HPV positive status of tumor (for oropharyngeal cancer) and Epstein barr virus (EBV) positive status (for nasopharyngeal cancer), tumor site and stage at the time of diagnosis, with the important factor being whether patient has metastatic involvement of the lymph nodes (1). ~1/3 rd of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSC) tend to relapse with locoregional recurrence. Second primary tumors are also common due to the concept of field cancerization. Presence of distant metastases or recurrence of tumor is associated with a poor prognosis given a median survival of ~6-8 months (1). Advances in the management of HNC has not resulted in a significant improvement in the 5-year survival rate which is ~40%-50% (2). Rosenberg et al's (3) study among recurrent/metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) reports a real world OS (rwOS) of 7.8 months (95% CI: 7.0-8.4). Median rwOS was significantly longer for the HPV-related (9.3 months, 95%CI: 8.2-10.9) vs HPV-unrelated group (6.8 months, 95%CI: 6.1-7.3), HR: 0.85 (95%CI: 0.73-0.99, p=0.036).Yang et al (4) in their review infer that it is imperative to identify the molecular markers which are associated with the biological behavior of HNC for predicting its prognosis. In this context, COX-2 is a potential prognostic factor for predicting survival in cancer patients. COX-2 is an inducible enzyme which serves as an indicator of inflammation rather than a systemic marker. It is not a serum marker like the acute phase protein 'CRP'. It is localized to tissues and cannot be searched systemically. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the technique used to detect the expression of COX-2. This viewpoint article aims to synthesize the feasibility of repurposing COX-2 inhibition as a strategic treatment approach for HNC.The two isoforms of cyclooxygenase (COX) include COX-1 and COX-2. Most cells express the enzyme COX-1, which in-turn facilitates several physiological functions such as the synthesis of mucosal lining in the stomach and aggregation of platelets. COX-2 is less widely expressed and is mainly found in the stomach, kidney, central nervous system and female reproductive tract. Different stimuli which can induce COX-2 in other cell types include growth factors, cytokines, carcinogens, oncogenes, and chronic inflammation. Carcinogenesis has been linked to an increased expression of COX-2 (1).The carcinogenic potential of COX-2 is reflected not just by its expression, but by the mediated downstream pro-inflammatory products such as prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). The PGE2 levels were significantly induced in various cancer types including OSC. The expression of COX-2 in the normal oral mucosa is low and is induced by exposure to tobacco and other carcinogens. There is a 4-fold increased expression of COX-2 messenger RNA (mRNA) in the normal oral mucosa of smokers than non-smokers, and a 50-fold increase in oral cancer tissues than para-cancer areas (1). Among potentially malignant lesions such as oral lichen planus (OLP), evidence shows significantly higher levels of PGE2 compared with the control group (1).The activation of tumor associated inflammation is closely related to the activation of COX-2 pathway (5). Evidence shows the upregulation of COX-2 from healthy (3%) to premalignant lesions (41%) to oral carcinomas (88%) (6). COX-2 is known to play a role in the transformation from lower to higher grades of pre-malignancies as well as the behavior of invasive carcinomas, where its higher expression correlates with worse clinical outcomes. Prior evidence indicates the downregulation of COX as a strategy for preventing cancer, however further clinical studies should elucidate the benefits in invasive carcinomas. Table 1 lists the available evidence on the association of COX-2 and cancer.The multiple mechanisms of action of COX-2/PGE2 signaling axis in tumorigenesis and progression includes cAMP/PKA, RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT and NF-kB (by binding to EP4 receptors). PGE2's role in immunosuppression in tumor microenvironment (TME) is through suppression of NK cell function and inducing the expression of myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and cancer stem cell (CSC) phenotypes. Celecoxib which is a selective COX-2 inhibitor not only reduces the production of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, but also influences various signaling pathways related to tumor growth (5). The manifestation of celecoxib in cancer research includes its dual effects of antiinflammatory and potential anti-cancer properties. It should be used at therapeutic doses and for a duration relevant to cancer treatment, towards off-setting the potential cardiovascular side-effects. i) This pre-clinical study infers that COX-2 inhibition has a chemopreventive effect, but its application as a treatment for HNC in a clinical setting requires further research, ii) Anti-neovascularization involving PGE2 and VEGF is not sufficient to inhibit tumor cell growth in HNC, iii) Differential anti-cancer effect of COX-2 inhibition in HNC is reflected by its effect on early stage cancer, iv) Patients in the celecoxib and methotrexate arm had a significantly longer PFS and OS compared to the intravenous cisplatin arm (median PFS: 101 vs 66 days, p=0.014, median OS: 249 vs 152 days, p=0.02), v) Indicates the beneficial effect of COX-2 inhibition for palliative chemotherapy in patients with metastatic, relapsed or inoperable HNSC, vi)COX-2 relates with radiosensitivity and platinum resistance of HNC. 3 Yang B, Jia L, Guo Q, Ren H, Hu Y, Xie T (4). 2026.Clinicopathological and prognostic significance of cyclooxygenase-2 expression in head and neck cancer: A meta-analysis. i) In-vitro studies show that inflammation induced COX-2 expression participates in the development and survival of cancers, ii) Targeting COX-2 seems to be an effective way to control HNC, iii) Research studies infer that inhibition of COX-2 has a reversal effect on cancer progression, iv) This meta-analysis infers that COX-2 expression was not significantly correlated with advanced tumor stage (OR: 1.23, 95% CI: 0.98-1.55, p=0.074). However, significance was found between COX-2 expression and high risk of lymph node metastasis (OR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.03-1.6, p=0.027) and advanced TNM stage (OR: 1.33, 95% CI: 1.06-1.66, p=0.015), v) Slight heterogeneity observed in these analyses was not significant (F=0%, p=0.636 for tumor stage, F=21.6%, p=0.202 for lymph node metastasis, F=0%, p=0.505 for TNM stage), vi) Combined HR for OS was 1.93 (95% CI: 1.29-2.9, p=0.001) indicating that COX-2 expression had a significantly poor survival effect on patients with HNC. COX-2 expression was a poor predictor for RFS (HR: 2.02, 95% CI: 1.0-4.08, p=0.05) as well as DFS rate (HR: 5.14, 95% CI: 2.84-9.31, p=0.00), vii) The heterogeneity reported for these outcomes was found to be significant (F=87.9%, p=0.0 for OS, F=82.5%, p=0.0 for RFS, F=61.6%, p=0.074 for DFS). Kuang B, Yang K, Zhong X et al (5) The TNM system which is used for prognostication of HNC accounts for <30% of the variation observed in the survival rates of HNC(4). The TNM system is based on anatomic information and does not reflect the biological heterogeneity of cancer. In this context, it is crucial to identify the molecular markers associated with the biological behavior of HNC which complements the TNM system. The anti-cancer ability of celecoxib includes its sensitization of tumors to conventional therapies, effective reprogramming of the immunosuppressive TME and influencing various signaling pathways related to tumor growth. The clinicopathological and prognostic role of COX-2 in HNC needs to be further explored. Future integration of COX-2 inhibitors into cancer treatment requires biomarker driven patient selection and clinical validation. Chronic inflammatory state in the TME causes the progression of malignant tumors. The inflammatory mediators not only induce angiogenesis and accelerate metastasis, but also lead to resistance of chemo/immunotherapy by reshaping the tumor immune microenvironment. Such chronic inflammation is closely related to the activation of COX-2 pathway. The tumor immune evasion mechanisms induced by COX-2/PGE2 signaling pathway include regulating the MDSCs, lymphocytes (CD8+ and CD4+ T cells), NK cells and antigen presenting cells (APCs) (7). Jin K et al's study (7) infers that COX2-PGE2 pathway induces PDL-1 expression and results in T-cell exhaustion. Evidence from mouse models indicate an effective inhibition of growth of the primary tumor when EP4 antagonists are combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade (7).The effective reprogramming of the immunosuppressive TME by celecoxib is through targeting the COX-2/PGE2 axis. Other mechanisms include inhibiting the immunosuppressive cells (Tregs, MDSCs, M2 macrophage polarization) and enhancing the infiltration of CD8+ T cells and its activity. Its synergistic enhancement of chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy, especially immune checkpoint blockade, stems primarily from disrupting this critical axis thereby overcoming key mechanisms of treatment resistance and immune evasion (5). The unique activity of celecoxib exists at the intersection of inflammation, metabolism and immunity. Emerging research areas should explore how celecoxib induced metabolic shifts interact synergistically with immune signaling pathways to create a relaxed environment for effector cells.Celecoxib apart from the mentioned inhibitory action on the COX-2/PGE2 signaling pathway, also reduces the expression of vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF), suppress the growth and metastasis of HNC cells and decrease the PGE2 mediated immune escape mechanisms. Evidence also shows its effects in inhibiting the tumor associated inflammatory factors (eg: COX-2, IL-6, TGF-β) and modulating the function of MDSCs (5). In-vitro research indicates the anti-cancer effects of celecoxib on PIK3CA-mutated HNC cells through stress of the endoplasmic reticulum, reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial dysfunction (5). The role of celecoxib in personalized treatment modalities is defined by potential biomarkers such as COX-2 status of the tumor, germline genetic variants and sex specific factors.COX-2 has been viewed from the lens of molecular pathology in HNC, however its translational clinical application subsists as a therapeutic target. The current evidence base is reliant on heterogenous data and early phase studies, which precludes inclusion to the treatment regimen. Research has proved the association between high level of COX-2 expression and adverse clinicopathological characteristics as well as poor prognosis. The clinical application of COX-2 inhibitors as targeted therapy in HNC is confronted by challenges such as redundancy of downstream pathways, difference in the levels of biomarkers across groups, and potential cardiovascular side effects (8).By encapsulating celecoxib or combining it with other drugs (eg: gemcitabine, immunomodulators) in nanoparticles, the tumor specific targeting process is enhanced. Thus its offtarget effects are minimized (mitigation of CV risk) and the localized high dose effects are potentially achieved, which is a critical component for effective TME remodeling (5). For identifying the subgroups of patients likely to benefit, it is important to assess the dynamic rather than the static COX-2 expression. This includes monitoring the circulating factors (eg: VEGF reflecting angiogenesis/ inflammatory regulation and IL-8), single-cell sequencing to analyze the dynamic changes in immune cell subsets within TME, and functional testing using patient derived 3D organoid models capable of predicting the real-time treatment response. This enables shifting the paradigm from a single modality to a personalized combination therapy, defining the optimal timing, sequence and dosage of celecoxib in a complex multimodal protocol (5).Elevated COX-2 expression in the tissue is an indication of inflammation and has also been documented in premalignant lesions of the oral cavity. Evidence shows the involvement of COX-2 in the initiation and promotion of several solid tumors including HNC. COX-2 is acknowledged to play a vital role in the tumorigenesis related processes such as apoptosis, angiogenesis and immunomodulation (1). Thus, there exists scope for COX-2 inhibitors in increasing the overall response rate of HNC patients, as targeted therapeutics or as adjuvant therapeutics. Research avenues include the role of COX-2 in cancer including its prognosis, and the evidence from clinical trials which will enable better patient outcomes. This viewpoint article synthesizes evidence on the anti-tumor efficacy of celecoxib, both as a monotherapy and as a multimodal regimen. Its versatile functions are reflected by its effective elimination of key barriers to anti-tumor immunity.Author contributions: RN: Technical inputs, monitoring and reviewing the final draft, VR: Information synthesis and initial drafting, AS: conceptualization of the idea, validation and providing resources for the project.

Presence of distant metastases or recurrence of tumor is associated with a poor prognosis given a median survival of ~6-8 months (1). Rosenberg et al's (3) study among recurrent/metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) reports a real world OS (rwOS) of 7.8 months (95% CI: 7.0-8.4). COX-2 is known to play a role in the transformation from lower to higher grades of pre-malignancies as well as the behavior of invasive carcinomas, where its higher expression correlates with worse clinical outcomes. title: Testosterone-Based Gender-Affirming Hormone Therapy, Menopause, and Menopause Hormone Therapy: Implications for Reproductive Tract Immunity and Viral Pathogenesis
abstract: Sex hormones shape reproductive tract immunity and influence host defense against viral infection. However, much of our understanding of hormone-mediated immunity derives from cisgender populations and systemic studies. Comparatively less is known about the effects of sustained hormonal change within reproductive tissues. This gap is particularly relevant to transgender men (TGM) taking testosterone-based gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) and to menopausal women using menopause hormone therapy (MHT). Although biologically distinct, these populations provide complementary contexts for examining how sustained androgen exposure, ovarian hormone decline, and therapeutic hormone use influence reproductive tract immunity. In this review, we examine hormone-associated changes in reproductive tract epithelial, stromal, and immune cells including the reproductive tract microbiome and virome. We consider their implications for the acquisition, replication, persistence and pathogenesis of HIV-1, HPV, HSV and CMV. Understanding these tissue specific, hormone-immune-virus interactions may help identify gaps in viral prevention, screening, vaccination, and treatment efforts across diverse hormonal and reproductive contexts.

title: Vaginal Lactobacillus, HPV genotype and cervical lesions
abstract: Cervical cancer is strongly associated with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, while vaginal Lactobacillus may protect cervical health. This cross-sectional study included 65 women attending Bangladesh Medical University from September 2023 to September 2024. Vaginal swabs were analyzed for Lactobacillus colony counts and HPV genotyping using standard microbiological and molecular methods. Significant differences in Lactobacillus counts were observed among groups (p = 0.01), with HPV DNA detected in 66.2% and significantly associated with Lactobacillus levels (p = 0.02). Thus, altered vaginal Lactobacillus was associated with HPV infection and cervical lesions, suggesting potential utility as a biomarker for cervical cancer prevention.

title: HPV Types and Cytopathological Abnormalities in HPV Vaccination-Eligible Young Women in Brazil
abstract: Background/Objectives. About ten years after the introduction of quadrivalent (q) HPV vaccination for children and adolescents in Brazil, reductions in the prevalence of vaccine-targeted HPV types, qHPV types,(6, 11, 16, and 18) and cytopathological abnormalities would be expected. We evaluated HPV genotypes associated with cytopathological abnormalities in the HPV vaccination-eligible population. We included 300 women aged 18–24 years, vaccinated (n = 155) and unvaccinated (n = 145). Thirty-five HPV genotypes were investigated, and cytopathological abnormalities were classified according to the Bethesda System. In vaccination-eligible population, HPV infection was detected in 47.0%, at least one high-risk (HR) HPV type in 36.3%, HR non-qHPV types (excluding HPV16/18) in 36% and HR qHPV types (HPV16/18) in 0.3%, with no significant differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated women. Cytopathological abnormalities occurred in 42.7% of vaccination-eligible population, including 37.7% with low-grade and 5.0% with high-grade abnormalities. Vaccination was associated with a lower prevalence of cytopathological abnormality (aPR = 0.75; 95% CI: 0.58–0.98; p = 0.035). Cytological abnormalities were present in 81.5% of HR non-qHPV-positive samples. HR non-qHPV types accounted for 68.8% of all cytological abnormalities, 64.6% of low-grade abnormalities, and 100% of high-grade abnormalities, and were more prevalent in high-grade than in low-grade abnormalities (PR = 1.55; 95% CI: 1.35–1.77; p = 0.003) in the vaccine-eligible population. HR HPV types targeted only by the nonavalent vaccine (HPV31, 33, 45, 52, and/or 58) were present exclusively in 20.0% of high-grade abnormalities. No high-grade abnormalities occurred with low-risk HPV alone. Low frequencies of qHPV-targeted types and fewer cytopathological abnormalities among vaccinated patients suggest benefits of the vaccination. However, the current profile of HPV genotypes associated with cytopathological abnormalities was characterized by a predominance of HR non-qHPV types, including nonavalent vaccine-targeted types, with cytological abnormalities remaining frequent among patients infected with these genotypes.

title: Misconceptions About HPV Vaccination, Testing, and Cervical Cancer Prevention Among Female Health-Science Students in Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is the principal cause of cervical cancer. Vaccination and screening are effective, and health professionals play a key role in promoting their uptake in the community. Knowledge gaps among future health professionals may therefore limit their ability to counsel patients and families. This study assessed knowledge of HPV infection, vaccination, testing, and cervical cancer prevention among female health-science students at Taif University, identified common misconceptions, and examined predictors of adequate knowledge. Methods: From February to May 2026, 394 female students in four different health programs completed a cross-sectional questionnaire containing 32 knowledge-based items across four domains: general HPV, HPV testing, HPV vaccination, and Saudi vaccine/program knowledge. Correct responses scored 1; incorrect and “I don’t know” responses scored 0; and two items with context-dependent answers were excluded, giving a 30-item score (range: 0–30). Scores ≥50% indicated adequate knowledge; stricter cut-offs (≥60% and ≥70%) and a guessing-corrected score were tested in sensitivity analyses. Analyses included descriptive statistics, non-parametric comparisons, chi-square tests, internal consistency, and multivariable logistic regression using Python 3.12. Results: The mean score was 13.09 ± 7.11, and the median was 15 (IQR: 8–18). A total of 193 students (49.0%) had a low level of knowledge, and 201 (51.0%; 95% CI: 46.1–55.9) had adequate knowledge. HPV testing had the lowest domain score (31.4% of the maximum possible score). Internal consistency was high (KR-20/Cronbach’s alpha = 0.898). Senior students had greater odds of having adequate knowledge (AOR = 2.66, 95% CI: 1.47–4.81; p = 0.001). Radiology students had greater odds than Medical Laboratory students (AOR = 2.19, 95% CI: 1.20–4.00; p = 0.011). Sensitivity analyses supported the association with senior academic stage, but not the radiology association. With a stricter ≥60% cut-off, only 29.4% of students had adequate knowledge. Conclusions: HPV-related knowledge was suboptimal, particularly that relating to HPV testing and vaccination. The association with senior academic stage supports the idea of introducing HPV and cervical cancer education earlier across health programs.

title: HPV-Independent Gastric-Type Endocervical Adenocarcinoma Diagnosed After Hysteroscopic Polypectomy: A Case Report
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Gastric-type adenocarcinoma (GAS) is the most common human papillomavirus (HPV)-independent adenocarcinoma of the cervix. Because it arises deep in the endocervical canal, can look deceptively bland, and is not detected by HPV testing, its diagnosis is often delayed. Case Presentation: A 57-year-old woman had six months of postmenopausal bleeding. At a local hospital, a Pap smear was read as atrophic vaginitis, and her bleeding improved after hysteroscopic polypectomy and curettage. One week later, surveillance computed tomography for a resected benign mesenteric tumor incidentally showed a 2.7 × 2.6 cm cervical mass. High-risk HPV testing was negative, CA19-9 rose from 42 to 73 U/mL (5.2 U/mL after surgery), and biopsy showed adenocarcinoma in situ. Radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy revealed a 3.3 cm HPV-independent GAS with deep-third stromal invasion, no lymphovascular invasion, and 25 negative nodes (FIGO 2018 stage IB2). The tumor was p16-negative, ER/PR-negative, and diffusely CK7-positive, with null-pattern p53 staining. No adjuvant therapy was given. Conclusions: This case adds a documented interval of one week between polypectomy and CT detection of a 2.7 cm tumor, the course of CA19-9 around surgery, and the reasoning for observation without adjuvant therapy in stage IB2 disease. Improvement of bleeding after polypectomy did not exclude a coexisting cervical mass; when sampling is limited or clinical, imaging, and pathological findings are discordant, the evaluation should continue. A negative HPV test, mildly elevated CA19-9, and a p16-negative, p53-aberrant mucinous adenocarcinoma are supportive but nonspecific clues that should prompt consideration of GAS, not establish it.

title: Trends in high-grade cervical lesions and Cancer following school-based and catch-up HPV vaccination in northern Norway
abstract: Norway introduced school-based human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for 12-year-old girls in 2009 and a catch-up programme for women born in 1991–1996 during 2016–2019. We examined population-level trends in HPV16, HPV18, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+), CIN3+, and cervical cancer among women aged 25–28 and 29–34 years in Troms and Finnmark. This retrospective repeated cross-sectional study used anonymised, aggregated pathology data from the University Hospital of North Norway, the sole pathology provider for the region. Annual detection rates per 1000 screened women were analysed for 2009–2025; HPV16/18 analyses covered 2016–2025. Temporal trends were assessed by linear regression, and vaccination coverage was estimated ecologically from birth-cohort eligibility and national coverage data. The study included 90,997 annual woman-records, 4009 CIN2+, 1568 CIN3+, and 65 cervical cancers. From 2017 to 2025, CIN2+ declined from 76.5 to 28.2 per 1000 and CIN3+ from 28.6 to 5.8 among women aged 25–28 years. Corresponding declines among women aged 29–34 years were from 46.3 to 24.3 and from 20.6 to 7.2 per 1000, respectively. HPV16 and HPV18 declined markedly in the younger group; HPV16 also declined significantly in the older group, whereas HPV18 did not. Increasing cohort-level vaccination coverage coincided with substantial reductions in vaccine-type HPV and high-grade cervical lesions, with the largest declines among cohorts predominantly offered school-based vaccination.

title: Immunogenicity and acute reactogenicity of the 9-valent HPV vaccine in Chinese females aged 16–32 years: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The nine-valent human papillomavirus (9vHPV) vaccine offers broad protection against HPV-related diseases. However, its multidimensional safety profile-integrating acute hemodynamic changes, injection-site pain, local inflammatory reactions, and vasovagal responses-remains incompletely characterized. Validated tools for individualised risk prediction are also lacking. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study analysed routinely collected data from 103 females aged 16-32 years who completed the three-dose 9vHPV vaccination schedule (0-2-6 months) between January 2023 and January 2024. Participants were stratified into three age groups: 16-20 (n = 36), 21-26 (n = 33), and 27-32 years (n = 34). Immunogenicity was assessed by geometric mean titers (GMT) and seropositive rates (SPR) for all nine HPV types one month after dose three. Safety outcomes included acute hemodynamic changes (heart rate, blood pressure), injection-site pain (Visual Analog Scale), local inflammatory reactions, systemic adverse events following immunisation (AEFI), and vasovagal reactions. Multidimensional correlation analyses, K-means clustering, temporal scan statistics, and an exploratory logistic regression-based risk prediction models were applied. RESULTS: All nine HPV types achieved SPR ≥98.1% (range 98.1-100%), with GMT ranging from 2832 to 16,875 mIU/mL. The 16-20 years group showed significantly higher GMTs than the 27-32 years group for multiple types (e.g., HPV16: +61.1%, P = 0.010). Acute hemodynamic changes included heart rate elevation in 83.5% of participants, with 98.1% normalising within 30 min. Injection-site pain peaked immediately post-vaccination (VAS 3.8 ± 2.1) and was predominantly mild to moderate (87.4%). Heart rate elevation correlated significantly with pain intensity (Spearman ρ = 0.706, P 85 bpm was an independent predictor of vasovagal reactions (OR = 3.20, P = 0.008), while younger age and lower BMI were significantly associated with the vasovagal-sensitive phenotype. CONCLUSIONS: In this preliminary retrospective cohort, the 9vHPV vaccine induced robust immunogenicity across the 16-32 years age range with no vaccine-related serious adverse events. Acute hemodynamic changes and vasovagal reactions were transient and mostly mild, and were likely influenced by procedural and autonomic factors rather than vaccine components alone. This study provides preliminary integrated evidence linking acute hemodynamic, pain, and local inflammatory responses after 9vHPV vaccination and introduces an internally validated, exploratory risk stratification tool. External validation in unselected real-world cohorts is required before clinical implementation.

abstract_zh: 背景:九价 人乳头瘤病毒 (9vHPV) 疫苗 可针对 HPV 相关疾病提供广泛的保护。然而,其多维安全性——整合急性血流动力学变化、注射部位疼痛、局部炎症反应和血管迷走反应——仍未完全表征。还缺乏经过验证的个性化风险预测工具。方法:这项回顾性 队列研究 研究分析了 103 名 16-32 岁女性的常规收集数据,这些女性在 2023 年 1 月至 2024 年 1 月期间完成了三剂 9vHPV 疫苗接种 计划(0-2-6 个月)。参与者被分为三个年龄组:16-20(n = 36)、21-26(n = 33) 和 27-32 岁 (n = 34)。在第三剂给药后一个月,通过所有九种 HPV 类型的几何平均滴度 (GMT) 和血清阳性率 (SPR) 评估免疫原性。安全性结果包括急性血流动力学变化(心率、血压)、注射部位疼痛(视觉模拟量表)、局部炎症反应、免疫后全身不良事件(AEFI)和血管迷走神经反应。应用了多维相关分析、K 均值聚类、时间扫描统计和基于探索性逻辑回归的风险预测模型。结果:所有九种 HPV 类型均达到 SPR ≥98.1%(范围 98.1-100%),GMT 范围为 2832 至 16,875 mIU/mL。对于多种类型,16-20 岁组的 GMT 显着高于 27-32 岁组(例如 HPV16:+61.1%,P = 0.010)。83.5% 的参与者出现急性血流动力学变化,其中心率升高,其中 98.1% 在 30 分钟内恢复正常。注射部位疼痛在 疫苗接种 后立即达到峰值 (VAS 3.8 ± 2.1),主要为轻度至中度 (87.4%)。心率升高与疼痛强度显着相关(Spearman ρ = 0.706,P 85 bpm 是血管迷走神经反应的独立预测因子(OR = 3.20,P = 0.008),而较年轻的年龄和较低的 BMI 与血管迷走神经敏感表型显着相关。结论:在这项初步回顾性 队列研究 中,9vHPV 疫苗 在 16-32 岁年龄范围内诱导强大的免疫原性,没有与 疫苗 相关的严重不良事件。急性血流动力学变化和血管迷走反应是短暂的,大多是轻微的,并且可能受到程序和自主因素的影响,而不是单独的 疫苗 成分的影响。本研究提供了 9vHPV 疫苗接种 后急性血流动力学、疼痛和局部炎症反应之间联系的初步综合证据,并引入了内部验证的探索性风险分层工具。在临床实施之前,需要在未选择的真实世界 队列研究 中进行外部验证。

title: HPV positivity, genotype distribution, age-specific patterns, and frequency of multiple infections among 8,209 women in a referral population: a retrospective study
abstract: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) causes cervical cancer, and regional data on circulating genotypes are needed to interpret local HPV epidemiology. We aimed to describe HPV positivity, genotype distribution, age-specific patterns and the frequency of multiple infections among women referred for HPV genotyping in Shiraz, southern Iran. This retrospective cross-sectional study used records extracted from patients’ files of women aged ≥ 18 years referred by physicians to a referral molecular laboratory in Shiraz during 1399–1403 (Iranian calendar; approximately March 2020 to March 2025); the referral indication was not recorded. DNA was extracted and HPV was genotyped with commercial kits that varied over time; the set of genotypes reported differed between calendar years. Genotypes in IARC Groups 1, 2 A and 2B were classified as high-risk (HR) and all others as low-risk (LR), and each woman was assigned to one mutually exclusive category (HPV-negative, HR-only, LR-only, or mixed HR/LR). Multiple infection was defined as ≥ 2 different genotypes in one sample. Associations with age were tested using the Pearson chi-square test and linear-by-linear association, and co-detection of HR–LR genotype pairs was assessed descriptively using Fisher's exact tests on the 2×2 table of each pair, an age-stratified exact test and Holm adjustment across 418 pairs. We analyzed 8,209 women. HPV positivity was 34.2% (95% CI 33.2–35.3%); HR-only, LR-only and mixed HR/LR infections were detected in 21.8%, 5.4% and 6.9% of women, respectively, any high-risk genotype (HR-only or mixed) was detected in 28.8% (95% CI 27.8–29.8%) and 42.5% (1,193/2,809) of HPV-positive women had multiple genotypes. title: Long-term trends and future projections of cervical cancer burden in China, 1990–2023: a Global Burden of Disease 2023 analysis
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Cervical cancer remains a major public health challenge among women in China. This study aimed to comprehensively assess long-term trends and future projections of cervical cancer burden in China. METHODS: Data on cervical cancer in China from 1990 to 2023 were extracted from Global Burden of Disease Study2023. Prevalence, incidence, deaths, years lived with disability (YLDs), years of life lost (YLLs), disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), and age-standardized rates (ASRs) were analyzed. Temporal trends were evaluated using estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) and Joinpoint regression. Das Gupta decomposition quantified the contributions of population growth, aging, and epidemiological change. Nordpred was used to project deaths and DALYs from 2024 to 2045. RESULTS: From 1990 to 2023, prevalent cervical cancer cases increased from 445,795 (95% uncertainty interval [UI]=301,749-642,609) to 752,306 (95% UI=481,273 to 1,011,544). YLDs increased by 62%, whereas YLLs decreased by 4%. Overall DALYs decreased slightly from 1,457,115 (95% UI=1,070,025 to 2,064,940) to 1,430,054 (95% UI=896,628 to 1,874,757), while deaths increased by 16%. Age-standardized DALYs rate (ASDR) declined from 294.14 to 132.72 per 100,000 population, with an EAPC of -2.43 (95% confidence interval=-2.54 to -2.33). Decomposition showed that population aging and growth offset favorable epidemiological changes, and projections suggested continued declines in ASDR with relatively stable deaths through 2045. CONCLUSION: Despite sustained declines in ASRs, the absolute burden of cervical cancer in China remains considerable due to demographic shifts. These findings underscore the urgent need to strengthen human papillomavirus vaccination coverage and expand equitable cervical cancer screening programs.

title: Comparative performance of three HPV DNA detection assays for cervical cancer screening in Algeria
abstract: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is the principal etiological driver of cervical cancer, making accurate HPV detection central to contemporary screening strategies. This study compared three molecular assays-INNO-LiPA HPV Genotyping Extra, Cobas 4800 HPV, and Amplicor HPV-using overlapping cervical-sample subsets from Algerian women at increased risk of cervical disease. Among the 94 specimens tested by both INNO-LiPA and Cobas, HR-HPV was detected in 54.3% and 29.8%, respectively; INNO-LiPA also identified HPV16 and HPV18 more frequently. In the 18-specimen subset tested by all three assays, HR-HPV positivity was 27.8% with INNO-LiPA, 33.3% with Cobas, and 50.0% with Amplicor. Pairwise agreement ranged from weak to substantial (κ=0.116-0.667), and discordance was significantly associated with multiple HPV infections (OR=5.88, 95% CI 1.29-26.85; p=0.012). HR-HPV positivity was more frequent in specimens with abnormal cytology, with the strongest association observed for INNO-LiPA (OR=4.9, 95% CI 1.5-15.9; p=0.005). Using the study-defined composite reference classification, INNO-LiPA showed higher sensitivity (93%) but lower specificity (62%) than Cobas (71% and 88%, respectively). These findings demonstrate substantial assay-dependent variation in HR-HPV detection and highlight the value of detailed genotyping for epidemiological investigation, while supporting the use of clinically validated HR-HPV assays for screening applications.

title: Histopathological Confirmation of Clinically Suspected HPV-Associated Papillary Lesions of the Oral Mucosa: A Prospective Study of 37 Cases
abstract: Background/Objectives: Benign papillary lesions of the oral mucosa are commonly attributed to human papillomavirus (HPV), yet reactive, neoplastic and potentially malignant lesions may present with a similar clinical appearance. Evidence on how frequently a clinical suspicion of an HPV-associated papillary lesion is confirmed histopathologically derives mainly from retrospective series encompassing the entire spectrum of oral pathology. The present study aimed to estimate this proportion prospectively within a single, predefined lesion category. Methods: Thirty-seven consecutive patients examined at a single center between October 2024 and May 2026 were enrolled. Before excisional biopsy, a single examiner recorded a clinical diagnosis of a suspected HPV-associated papillary lesion according to predefined criteria, and one index lesion per patient was examined. Concordance was defined as a histopathological diagnosis of squamous papilloma, verruca vulgaris, condyloma acuminatum or multifocal epithelial hyperplasia, established on morphological grounds without HPV testing. The concordance rate is reported with an exact 95% confidence interval (CI); concordant and discordant cases were compared in an exploratory analysis using the Mann–Whitney U and Fisher’s exact tests. Results: The cohort comprised 21 women and 16 men, with a mean age of 41.8 ± 15.8 years. The clinical diagnosis was confirmed in 30 of 37 cases (81.08%; 95% CI 64.84–92.04%), with squamous papilloma as the predominant diagnosis (23 cases). All seven discordant lesions were benign, most frequently fibroma (four cases), and no epithelial dysplasia was reported in any specimen. No variable was significantly associated with concordance, although these comparisons were markedly underpowered. Conclusions: In this selected population, approximately one clinical suspicion in five was not confirmed. The estimate represents the positive predictive value of an institutionally defined clinical category in a selected population, based on morphological rather than molecular confirmation; it does not reflect overall diagnostic accuracy, and its generalizability is limited by the wide CI and the single-center design. Histopathological examination therefore remains indispensable for a definitive diagnosis.

title: The RNA-binding protein YWHAG influences cervical cancer progression and immune microenvironment
abstract: Introduction Cervical cancer (CC) is one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths among women worldwide. The roles of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) in regulating alternative splicing (AS) and the tumor microenvironment (TME) in CC are not well understood. This study investigated the associations between prognosis‐ and immune‐related RBPs and CC progression. Materials and methods Bioinformatics data were retrieved from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx), and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Prognosis- and immune-related RBPs were identified using univariate Cox regression analysis and CIBERSORT. AS events were analyzed via Splice Site Usage Variation Analysis (SUVA). Gene Ontology (GO) terms and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways were used to categorize gene functions. Immune cell infiltration was inferred with CIBERSORT and ssGSEA. Correlations between YWHAG and immune-related genes were examined with Sangerbox and TISIDB web tools. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis was performed on GSE168652. Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), western blot (WB) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were performed to quantify the candidate RBPs in clinical tissues. Functional experiments including CCK-8, colony formation, wound-healing, transwell invasion and migration, and cell apoptosis were conducted to explore the biological role of YWHAG. Results Using RNA sequencing data from TCGA, we identified 14 prognosis-related RBPs and 13 immune-related RBPs. Differentially expressed RBPs were associated with numerous AS events, correlating with CC progression. 14-3-3γ (YWHAG) was significantly upregulated in cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) and correlated with shorter progression-free interval (PFI) across multiple cohorts. In vitro assays demonstrated that YWHAG exerts consistent oncogenic activity in both HPV-positive SiHa and HPV-negative C33A cell lines of CSCC. YWHAG was positively correlated with macrophage infiltration while inversely associated with multiple T-cell subsets on TCGA bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq, and related to multiple immune-modulatory genes like PD-L1. Discussion YWHAG serves as a key prognostic and immune-regulator in CC, and contribute to cancer progression, possibly linked to AS‐dependent immune microenvironment reprogramming. Targeting YWHAG may be a promising therapeutic strategy for CC.

title: Computational discovery of potential HPV E6 and E7 binders from Lissachatina fulica slime for oral squamous cell carcinoma therapeutics
abstract: CONTEXT: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is primarily driven by the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 which promote malignant progression through inactivation of the tumour suppressors p53 and retinoblastoma protein. This study investigated 26 bioactive metabolites from the slime of Lissachatina fulica as computationally predicted binders of HPV16 E6 and E7 proteins. Among identified metabolites, the drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic, toxicity profiles were further evaluated along with two reference compounds Curcumene and Melphalan. Nineteen compounds satisfied the screening criteria were subjected to molecular docking against HPV16 E6 and E7 proteins. The highest-ranking complexes were further evaluated by molecular dynamics simulations. Phenol, 2,4-bis(1,1-dimethylethyl)- formed the most stable complex with HPV16 E6 whereas (16R,17S)-10,10,16,17-tetramethyl-6-phenyl- and calophyllolide exhibited the greatest stability with HPV16 E7 highlighting L. fulica slime as a putative source of candidate molecules for further experimental investigation against HPV-associated OSCC. METHODS: Twenty-six metabolites identified from L. fulica slime were screened for drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic and toxicity properties using SwissADME and ProTox-3.0. Nineteen compounds satisfying the screening criteria were docked against HPV16 proteins using AutoDock Vina with Curcumene and Melphalan as reference compounds. The highest-ranked protein-ligand complexes were subjected to 500 ns extended molecular dynamics simulations using the GROMACS package with the CHARMM27 force field. Trajectory analyses included root mean square deviation (RMSD), root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), radius of gyration (Rg), solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), and hydrogen-bond analysis.

title: Fathers’ Intention to Vaccinate Their Adolescent Sons Against HPV: A Structural Equation Model Based on the IMB Model
abstract: Background/Objectives: Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes various cancers in both sexes, yet HPV vaccination uptake among adolescent boys in South Korea remains notably low. Despite the importance of parental decision-making, fathers’ roles in HPV vaccination have been understudied. This study identified factors influencing fathers’ intentions to vaccinate their adolescent sons against HPV and tested a structural model based on the Information–Motivation–Behavioral Skills (IMB) model. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 253 fathers of sons aged 12–17 years in South Korea. Data were analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, and bootstrapping. Results: The hypothesized model demonstrated adequate fit (GFI = 0.97, AGFI = 0.90, SRMR = 0.05, RMSEA = 0.08, NFI = 0.95, TLI = 0.93, CFI = 0.97) and explained 43.7% of the variance in vaccination intention. Seven of 11 hypothesized paths were supported. Self-efficacy had the strongest direct effect on vaccination intention (β = 0.39), followed by subjective norms (β = 0.21), perceived barriers (β = −0.12), and attitudes toward HPV vaccination (β = 0.11). Self-efficacy fully mediated the relationship between knowledge and vaccination intention and partially mediated the effects of attitudes and subjective norms. Social support had no significant effect on self-efficacy or vaccination intention. Conclusions: These findings identify self-efficacy as a central mechanism underlying fathers’ HPV vaccination intentions. Father-targeted interventions may benefit from strengthening self-efficacy through practical guidance, while also addressing subjective norms, attitudes, and perceived barriers, to promote HPV vaccination among adolescent sons.

title: Patient Acceptance and Attitudes About Self-Sampling Versus Pap Smear for Cervical Cancer Screening: A Mixed Methods Study.
abstract: ObjectivesTo assess patient attitudes and acceptance of human papillomavirus (HPV) self-testing versus Papanicolaou (Pap) smear for early detection of uterine cervical neoplasms.MethodsThis convergent mixed methods study, conducted at a large academic health network in eastern Pennsylvania, utilized a questionnaire and semi-structured interviews to explore patient views on the acceptability (operationalized using Theoretical Framework of Acceptability constructs) of Pap smear and human papillomavirus self-testing. Population included adults aged 25 to 65 deemed average risk for cervical cancer.Results156 respondents with mean age 44±11.3 years, most college-educated (117/154, 76.0%), and not Hispanic (89/155, 57.4%). Overall acceptability scores for each technique were similar (28.2% self-sampling vs. Self-sampling scored significantly lower (all P < .001) for confidence obtaining a good sample (mean difference [MD] -0.48 [95% CI: -0.59, -0.37]), purpose for test (MD -0.21 [-0.27, -0.15]), and trust in accuracy (MD -0.35 [-0.43, -0.26]). Self-sampling was preferred for not painful (MD 0.13 [0.04, 0.22], P = .007), privacy (MD 0.31 [0.22, 0.40], P < .001), and convenience (MD 0.15 [0.04, 0.27], P = .01). Interview themes revealed self-sampling benefits (convenience, privacy, pain/comfort, empowering) and barriers (inability to perform test accurately, test burden, body modesty, age).ConclusionsParticipants did not prefer one screening method over another. Reinforcing convenience, privacy and effectiveness might increase uptake of self-sampling, while education on the risks of HPV progression to cervical cancer may increase cervical cancer screening rates overall.
journal: Journal of primary care & community health

title: SERPINA3 Expression in HPV-Infected Cervical Tissue
abstract: Persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) involve interactions between viral activity and host tissue responses. This secondary analysis assessed SERPINA3 expression in cervical tissue from 85 women and related it to HPV DNA status, genotype, lesion grade, and previously published quantitative E4 and L1 measurements from the same cohort and tissue material. Its added value is jointly evaluating a host protease inhibitor and two complementary markers of productive HPV infection, rather than assessing E4 or L1 alone. SERPINA3 was assessed by immunohistochemistry and digital image analysis. Associations were evaluated using Spearman rank correlation and Mann–Whitney U tests. No statistically significant associations were detected with L1, E4, ISH II, ISH III, age, HPV status, HPV16 status, or CIN diagnosis. The wide confidence intervals for subgroup comparisons limit the exclusion of potentially relevant differences. These exploratory findings do not establish SERPINA3 as a marker of productive HPV infection, and they neither demonstrate biological independence from HPV nor validate it as a marker of the cervical microenvironment. Cytokine signaling, epithelial composition, and local proteolytic regulation provide hypotheses for further investigation.

title: Pan-viral focused metagenomics reveals viral diversity in febrile patients from the Peruvian Amazon
abstract: Febrile illness (FI) remains a major diagnostic challenge in endemic regions exposed to diverse and emerging pathogens. Despite its high prevalence in Peru, the causative agent frequently remains unidentified. Here, we applied viral capture metagenomics to identify viral pathogens in patients with FI from the Loreto region of the Peruvian Amazon. Viruses were detected in 32.4% of samples, the most frequent families being Picornaviridae (35.7%), Orthoherpesviridae (19%), Flaviviridae (11.9%), Papillomaviridae (11.9%), Coronaviridae (11.9%), and Paramyxoviridae (7.1%). The recovered complete or near-complete viral genomes with coverage ≥ 90% ( n = 34) were of high quality, with a median genome coverage of 99.5% (range 90.5–100%; mean 97.9%) and a median depth of 331.3x (range 6.9x-20,274x; mean 1,828.8x). These data supported phylogenetic analyses that confirmed the circulation of clinically relevant genotypes, including Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus subtype ID, Panama/Peru genotype, dengue virus serotypes 1 and 3, enteroviruses D68 and C109, Coxsackieviruses A5 and A21, multiple HPV types, and human coronaviruses HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, and HCoV-OC43. Metagenomic sequencing showed 95.8% concordance with prior RT-qPCR-positive samples ( n = 48). Sample type and handling were critical for maximizing viral recovery and detection. Together, these findings reveal extensive viral diversity associated with FI in the Loreto region and support the usefulness of viral capture metagenomics for improving pathogen detection and genomic surveillance in endemic regions.
authors: Íris Terezinha Santos de Santana Silva

title: Burden and temporal trends of cervical cancer in reproductive-age females from 1990 to 2021 and projections to 2035 in G20 countries: a systematic analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Cervical cancer remains a critical global health threat. Despite its member states accounting for more than 85% of global gross domestic product (GDP), no comprehensive assessment of cervical cancer burden exists across the diverse Group of Twenty (G20) economies. This study aimed to characterize long-term cervical cancer burden trends and project future epidemiological trajectories among G20 reproductive-age females. METHODS: Using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, we analyzed cervical cancer disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) among females aged 15-49 years in G20 countries (1990-2021) via Joinpoint regression, health inequality indices, Das Gupta decomposition, and Bayesian age-period-cohort projection to 2035. RESULTS: In 2021, cervical cancer generated 2.27 million DALYs among G20 reproductive-age females, with age-standardized rates ranging from 24.89 (Saudi Arabia) to 667.65 (South Africa) per 100,000. Overall rates declined (annual average percent change [AAPC]=-1.40%) (1990-2021), with China achieving a notable reduction (AAPC=-1.51%), but increased in Russia (AAPC=1.70%), Japan (AAPC=0.65%), Italy (AAPC=0.33%), and South Africa (AAPC=0.14%). Sociodemographic Index (SDI)-related inequality narrowed (1990: Slope Index of Inequality [SII]=-349.58, Concentration Index=-0.21; 2021: SII=-261.82, Concentration Index=-0.18), but persisted. Population growth (+23.99%) and age structure changes (+20.92%) drove DALY increases in the G20, offset by epidemiological improvements (-43.92%). Most G20 countries will see declining burden by 2035, while South Africa faces the largest increase. CONCLUSION: Differentiated, evidence-based strategies tailored to national burden characteristics, addressing demographic shifts, key health system gaps, and human papillomavirus genotype disparities, are critically needed to successfully achieve the World Health Organization 2030 global cervical cancer elimination targets.

title: Invasive Cervical Carcinoma Detected Despite Negative Cytology: A Retrospective Cytology–Histopathology Correlation Study
abstract: Background: Conventional cytology remains widely used for cervical cancer screening; however, its sensitivity for detecting high-grade lesions and invasive disease is variable, particularly in symptomatic women.Objective: To evaluate cytology-histopathology discordance and quantify the occurrence of clinically significant cervical lesions, including invasive carcinoma, in women undergoing conventional cytology.Materials and methods: This retrospective study included 200 women aged 25-65 years who underwent conventional Pap smear screening followed by colposcopy and biopsy based on abnormal cytology and/or suspicious clinical findings at a tertiary care center.Cytology was reported according to the Bethesda System.Histopathological findings were correlated with cytology results.Associations were assessed using the Chi-square test.Results: Among 200 women, 157 (78.5%) had negative cytology (NILM).Histopathology revealed clinically significant lesions in 40 women (20.0%), including cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 1) in 8 (4.0%), CIN 2 in 2 (1.0%), and invasive carcinoma in 31 (15.5%).Notably, 21 of 31 carcinoma cases (67.7%) occurred in women with NILM cytology.Significant lesions were identified across NILM, atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS), Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), and inflammatory cytology categories (χ2 = 50.407,p = 0.001).Conclusion: Conventional cytology alone may be insufficient to exclude clinically significant cervical pathology in symptomatic women.Careful clinical evaluation and appropriate diagnostic assessment remain essential, particularly in settings where human papillomavirus (HPV)-based screening is not universally implemented.
journal: Journal of South Asian Federation of Obstetrics and Gynaecology

title: Collagen architectural disorganization on routine H&E images predicts survival and molecular states across 1664 head and neck squamous cell carcinomas
abstract: Survival outcomes in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remain heterogeneous despite established predictors such as TNM stage and human papillomavirus (HPV) status. Most prognostic models focus on tumor cell–intrinsic features, whereas the structural contribution of the tumor microenvironment remains underexplored. We quantified collagen architectural disorganization at the tumor–stroma interface on routine hematoxylin and eosin–stained whole-slide images using collagen disorder architecture (CoDA), a computational pathology framework. The multi-institutional cohort included 1664 patients with oral cavity, oropharyngeal, and laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma. CoDA-derived stromal features stratified overall and disease-free survival in an independent validation cohort and across the examined tumor subsites. CoDA-defined high-risk status remained associated with adverse outcomes after adjustment for clinicopathological variables, although model discrimination was modest. Transcriptomic profiling showed that CoDA high-risk tumors were associated with programs involving lineage plasticity, neuronal–neuroendocrine features, lipid metabolism, and immune modulation. Activated mast-cell and basophil signatures were enriched in high-risk tumors, whereas lymphocyte-associated immune-cell signatures did not differ after correction for multiple comparisons. These findings indicate that collagen architectural disorganization is associated with outcome and tumor states in HNSCC. CoDA may provide a complementary research biomarker derived from routine histopathology, although prospective validation is needed before application.

title: ADESÃO À VACINAÇÃO CONTRA O HPV EM ADOLESCENTES E O PAPEL DA ENFERMAGEM
abstract: O Papilomavírus Humano (HPV), transmitido principalmente por via sexual, afeta numerosos indivíduos em âmbito mundial, destacando-se em adolescentes. A vacinação contra o HPV é recomendada em várias diretrizes nacionais e internacionais, focando especialmente na imunização precoce para otimizar a sua eficácia. A vacinação contra o HPV, incluída no Calendário Nacional de Vacinação em 2014, continua sendo uma das principais medidas de prevenção primária contra as infecções pelo vírus. Diante disso, este é um estudo de revisão integrativa da literatura que teve como objetivos analisar na literatura a adesão à vacinação contra o HPV em adolescentes e descrever papel da Enfermagem na prevenção do HPV. A busca na literatura foi realizada em bases de dados, tais como a LILACS, BDENF e PUBMED, utilizando os descritores “Adolescência”, “Papillomavirus Humano”, “Vacinas” e “Enfermagem”. Foram estabelecidos como critérios de inclusão artigos originais, disponíveis na íntegra e gratuitamente, publicados nos idiomas português e inglês, no período de 2021 a 2026. Os resultados evidenciaram que o crescimento da conscientização e maior participação na vacinação sugerem que a educação em saúde é essencial para promover a saúde sexual e reprodutiva dos jovens. Ademais, ao diminuir o estigma e o medo relacionados ao HPV, essas estratégias ajudaram a promover um ambiente mais aberto e acolhedor para conversas sobre a vacinação. Conclui-se que a educação em saúde baseada em teorias de enfermagem desempenha um papel essencial na promoção da adesão à vacinação contra o HPV. O papel da Enfermagem, nesse contexto, vai além da simples aplicação da vacina, ele se torna facilitador de informações e apoio aos adolescentes, incentivando-os a tomar decisões conscientes e responsáveis sobre sua saúde.
journal: Revista Ibero-Americana de Humanidades, Ciências e Educação

title: Cuidar de si é um ato de amor: relato do outubro Rosa na Usina da Paz
abstract: This experience report describes a Pink October educational action carried out by nursing students on the prevention and early detection of breast and cervical cancer, using a digital platform for sending questions without name identification. The activity took place on October 21, 2026, at a community facility in Belém, Pará, Brazil, was planned with the 5W2H tool, and was developed in four stages: reception, dialogued presentation, a question activity via QR Code, and closing. Eleven questions were received, all sent by audio and transcribed by the platform itself, so that the team received them only as text, which preserved anonymity. The questions addressed the frequency of screening tests, breast warning signs, human papillomavirus, and vaccination. The absence of name identification may have encouraged questions related to intimacy, and the need for a cell phone limited access for part of the audience. It is concluded that digital tools can complement human contact without replacing it, and that health education is built, above all, through listening.

title: Tempering and few-shot calibration of pathology foundation models improve digital biomarker reproducibility across slide scanners
abstract: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved consistency in head-and-neck cancer human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal cancer microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate cancer grading and breast cancer phenotyping. This tempering method decreased cross-scanner prediction differences by 67.5% for HPV (95% CI 59.0-73.9%), 69.3% for MSI (95% CI 51.9-76.5%) and 63.4%-81.2% for breast signatures. Cross-scanner prostate grade agreement rose from 42.5% to 92.7%. Under full scanner-HPV confounding during training, AUROC fell from 0.80 to 0.68 with original model features but only from 0.86 to 0.84 with tempering. Unlike post hoc feature calibration, tempering used only public data yet matched or exceeded on-site calibration. These findings support tempering to reduce scanner dependence of pathology foundation models.

title: Digital health interventions and equity in STI prevention in key populations in Sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review protocol
abstract: Background Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) remain a major public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. The elevated burden of STI-related infections, including bacterial STIs (e.g., syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia) and viral STIs (human papillomavirus, herpes simplex virus, viral hepatitis B and C), focusing on sexual health or STI prevention, contributes significantly to morbidity, mortality and increased HIV transmission risk. In accordance with World Health Organization guidelines, key populations are defined as men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals (regardless of sex work status), female or male sex workers, people who inject drugs (PWID), and people in correctional facilities or incarcerated settings, alongside priority vulnerable populations (adolescents and young people aged 10–24 years). Digital health interventions (DHIs) offer innovative platforms to address these challenges; however, evidence syntheses examining digital interventions for non-HIV STIs and integrated STI/HIV co-prevention services across the care continuum for key populations and priority vulnerable populations in sub-Saharan Africa remain limited. Objective This scoping review aims to map digital health interventions targeting non-HIV STIs and integrated STI/HIV service delivery models across sub-Saharan Africa, while strictly excluding standalone HIV-only management tools (such as ART adherence platforms without STI components). Methods and analysis This scoping review will follow the framework of Arksey and O'Malley and incorporate refinements by Levac et al. and the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. A systematic search will be undertaken across major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and CINAHL. The Rayyan software platform will be used to eliminate duplicate records and facilitate double-blind study screening. Two independent reviewers will subsequently screen retrieved citations against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data will be extracted using a standardised charting form to capture intervention characteristics, target populations, digital modalities, structural health equity dimensions and qualitative and quantitative implementation outcomes. source_records.title: Digital health interventions and equity in STI prevention in key populations in Sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review protocol
source_records.abstract: Background Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) remain a major public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. The elevated burden of STI-related infections, including bacterial STIs (e.g., syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia) and viral STIs (human papillomavirus, herpes simplex virus, viral hepatitis B and C), focusing on sexual health or STI prevention, contributes significantly to morbidity, mortality and increased HIV transmission risk. In accordance with World Health Organization guidelines, key populations are defined as men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals (regardless of sex work status), female or male sex workers, people who inject drugs (PWID), and people in correctional facilities or incarcerated settings, alongside priority vulnerable populations (adolescents and young people aged 10–24 years). Digital health interventions (DHIs) offer innovative platforms to address these challenges; however, evidence syntheses examining digital interventions for non-HIV STIs and integrated STI/HIV co-prevention services across the care continuum for key populations and priority vulnerable populations in sub-Saharan Africa remain limited. Objective This scoping review aims to map digital health interventions targeting non-HIV STIs and integrated STI/HIV service delivery models across sub-Saharan Africa, while strictly excluding standalone HIV-only management tools (such as ART adherence platforms without STI components). Methods and analysis This scoping review will follow the framework of Arksey and O'Malley and incorporate refinements by Levac et al. and the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. A systematic search will be undertaken across major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and CINAHL. The Rayyan software platform will be used to eliminate duplicate records and facilitate double-blind study screening. Two independent reviewers will subsequently screen retrieved citations against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data will be extracted using a standardised charting form to capture intervention characteristics, target populations, digital modalities, structural health equity dimensions and qualitative and quantitative implementation outcomes. The selection process will be reported using a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram. Findings will be synthesised narratively to map the evidence base and identify critical research gaps.
