full_text: AbstractBackgroundGastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (GAS) is the most common HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma. It is characterized by diagnostic difficulty, resistance to chemoradiotherapy and a propensity for peritoneal spread.Case presentationA 68-year-old woman presented with chronic hypogastric pain and a large hydrometra. Cervical cytology and an initial biopsy were non-diagnostic. A repeat biopsy established GAS (CK7-positive; p16, CK20, CDX2, estrogen receptor and PAX8-negative; wild-type p53; negative high-risk HPV by PCR), FIGO 2018 stage IIB, with negative staging imaging. After concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy and brachytherapy, MRI showed only a 23% reduction of the tumor. Radical hysterectomy, delayed by six months, revealed residual tumor with omental and pelvic peritoneal metastases that had not been detected on staging imaging. She received five cycles of carboplatin–paclitaxel as first-line systemic therapy, complicated by grade 3 radiation proctitis, right ureteral and vesicovaginal fistulas, and severe hematologic toxicity. Eight months after completing chemotherapy, she developed malignant bowel obstruction from peritoneal progression. PD-L1 was negative (combined positive score 0). She died under palliative care 25 months after diagnosis.ConclusionsThis case illustrates the diagnostic pitfalls and radioresistance of GAS and its capacity for peritoneal spread. Together with a focused review of published locally advanced cases, it suggests that staging laparoscopy and earlier comprehensive biomarker testing deserve prospective evaluation.Keywords: case report, gastric-type adenocarcinoma, HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma, hydrometra, peritoneal carcinomatosis, radioresistance Patient informationA 68-year-old woman from southwestern Colombia, a homemaker, presented with an eight-month history of colicky hypogastric pain radiating to the lower limbs. She had no urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms and no abnormal genital bleeding. She had no comorbidities, regular medications or known allergies.Her obstetric history included four pregnancies, with three cesarean deliveries and one ectopic pregnancy. Menarche occurred at age 12 and menopause at age 48. Her surgical history included three cesarean sections, a right salpingectomy and an appendectomy. She had not received HPV vaccination, and her previous cervical screening had been normal.Her family history was notable for ovarian cancer in one sister and breast cancer in another. Clinical features suggestive of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome were not documented, and germline genetic testing was not performed. She lived with her husband, who was her main caregiver. Patient perspectiveThe patient was under palliative sedation when publication was proposed and could not provide her own account; her perspective was conveyed by her husband. According to him, she expressed frustration with the adverse course of her disease despite the intensity of her treatments. She valued the medical team’s honest communication about her prognosis and limited options, which allowed an informed transition to palliative care focused on comfort and dignity. Clinical findingsAt diagnosis, she had good functional status. An enlarged uterus was palpable 3 cm below the umbilicus, without ascites. Speculum examination showed an atrophic cervix without exophytic lesions. Rectovaginal examination revealed a barrel-shaped cervix with a 4-cm endocervical mass, involvement of the right parametrium up to its middle third and of the left parametrium at its insertion, and a normal rectovaginal septum. There were no palpable inguinal or supraclavicular lymph nodes. Hydronephrosis was absent. These findings corresponded to FIGO 2018 stage IIB. DiscussionThis case adds three observations to the GAS literature: documented diagnostic pitfalls, objectively measured radioresistance, and histologically confirmed peritoneal dissemination that had not been detected on staging imaging at diagnosis, although its timing cannot be established.Diagnostic pitfallsCervical cytology and a first biopsy were non-diagnostic in our patient, consistent with reports that HPV-based screening and cytology often miss GAS because of its HPV independence, bland cytology and deep endocervical growth (6, 7, 14). A large hydrometra in a postmenopausal woman, as in this case, has been described as a clue to GAS (15) and should prompt deeper sampling.Differential diagnosisBecause GAS shows gastric differentiation, MUC6 or HIK1083 expression alone does not establish cervical origin, and metastatic gastrointestinal or pancreatobiliary adenocarcinoma is the main differential diagnosis. No single marker is definitive. GAS is typically p16-negative or patchy and CK7-positive, with variable PAX8 and CK20 expression. SATB2 and CDX2 favor an intestinal origin, although CDX2 expression has been reported in some GAS (14).HNF4α has emerged as a sensitive marker of endocervical glandular neoplasms in tissue, with a sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 95% (16), and in alcohol-fixed cytology (17). However, HNF4α is also expressed in gastric, colorectal, pancreatic and biliary adenocarcinomas; its value lies in combination, as an HNF4α-positive, SATB2-negative and CDX2-negative profile favors an endocervical origin (16). Given the negative cytology in our patient, HNF4α immunocytochemistry may deserve evaluation as a tool to improve cytological detection of GAS. In our case, the CK7-positive, CK20-negative, CDX2-negative and p16-negative profile, negative high-risk HPV PCR, and negative endoscopy and abdominal imaging favored primary GAS. However, this profile does not by itself exclude an upper gastrointestinal or pancreatobiliary origin, and gastric-specific markers, SATB2 and HNF4α were not performed.Radioresistance and the role of surgeryThe 23% tumor reduction after complete chemoradiotherapy is consistent with the known radioresistance of GAS. Response rates to radiotherapy are 50% in GAS versus 81.8% in usual-type adenocarcinoma (4), and gastric-type histology independently predicts non-complete response to definitive radiotherapy (9). In a small series, surgery achieved remission after chemoradiotherapy failure (12), and a recent multicenter real-world study suggested that multimodal treatment including surgery may improve survival (18).These data support the rationale for surgery in our patient, although the sequence used is not standard for FIGO IIB disease. In our patient, chemoradiotherapy, brachytherapy and radical surgery were followed by severe toxicity (radiation proctitis, ureteral and vesicovaginal fistulas, major bleeding), and subsequent failure was peritoneal rather than pelvic. Whether additional pelvic treatment benefits selected patients with GAS cannot be determined from a single case.Peritoneal disseminationPeritoneal and omental metastases were confirmed histologically at surgery, 11 months after diagnosis, although abdominal MRI and chest CT at diagnosis had shown no extrapelvic disease. Because surgery was delayed approximately six months and post-treatment imaging was limited to the pelvis, it cannot be determined whether this disease was present but radiologically occult at diagnosis or developed during treatment and the subsequent delay. GAS shows a propensity for omental, peritoneal and adnexal spread, which is often found at initial surgery and may be missed by preoperative imaging (8, 19). Staging laparoscopy or peritoneal cytology before definitive chemoradiotherapy may therefore be a strategy worth evaluating in locally advanced GAS, but its yield and impact on management have not been studied in this population and cannot be inferred from our case.Prognostic factorsGAS carries a markedly worse prognosis than usual-type adenocarcinoma at every stage, with lower disease-specific survival and a higher rate of advanced-stage presentation (4, 8). Reported adverse factors include advanced FIGO stage, lymph node involvement, parametrial invasion, deep stromal invasion and lymphovascular space invasion (4, 8, 20). In the systematic review of 150 cases, five-year survival was 26.7% and recurrences were predominantly distant (6).Our patient combined several of these features: parametrial involvement at diagnosis, full-thickness stromal invasion and lymphovascular space invasion in the residual tumor, and peritoneal metastases at surgery. Her overall survival of 25 months is consistent with this high-risk profile.Molecular landscape and therapeutic targetsGAS harbors frequent TP53, CDKN2A and STK11 alterations, distinct from HPV-associated adenocarcinoma (21, 22). Several actionable biomarkers are emerging. Claudin 18 is expressed in most GAS with low positivity thresholds, 78% in one series (23), but in only about one third when the ≥75% threshold used for claudin 18.2-directed therapy in gastric cancer is applied (24). PD-L1 is positive by combined positive score in about 37% of cases (23), and reported rates of HER2 overexpression or amplification range from about 7% to 25%, varying with the testing method and scoring criteria (21, 23, 25, 26). In our patient, PD-L1 was negative (CPS 0) and HER2 was not assessed.Optimal systemic therapy for GAS is undefined, and current management follows general cervical cancer guidelines (27, 28). Fluoropyrimidine–platinum regimens have been proposed on the basis of the gastric phenotype, but no prospective comparative data support their superiority. HER2-directed therapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors selected by CPS and claudin 18.2-targeted agents remain investigational in GAS. The first randomized phase III trial specifically designed for GAS is ongoing (29). Our patient remained progression-free for about eight months after carboplatin–paclitaxel, suggesting some platinum sensitivity despite marked radioresistance. No GAS-specific surveillance recommendations exist.Strengths and limitationsThe main strength of this report is complete longitudinal documentation from diagnosis to death, including diagnostic pitfalls, radiologic response, histologic confirmation of peritoneal spread not detected on staging imaging, toxicity and end-of-life care, compared with published cases of similar stage and treatment.Several limitations apply. As a single case, it cannot establish causal relationships between treatment and outcome, nor the value of staging laparoscopy or of pelvic treatment intensification. The immunohistochemical panel was incomplete: gastric-specific markers (MUC6, HIK1083), SATB2 and HNF4α were not performed, so a metastatic upper gastrointestinal or pancreatobiliary origin cannot be excluded with certainty. HER2, mismatch repair proteins and molecular profiling were not performed, and germline testing was not done despite a family history of ovarian and breast cancer. Detailed radiotherapy and brachytherapy dosimetry was not available. Surgery was delayed six months, and whether peritoneal disease was present at diagnosis cannot be determined.Practical lessonsNegative cytology and a non-diagnostic superficial biopsy do not exclude GAS; a deep endocervical mass or a large hydrometra in a postmenopausal woman should prompt repeat or deeper sampling.Conventional imaging may underestimate peritoneal spread in GAS (8, 19); whether staging laparoscopy or peritoneal cytology before definitive chemoradiotherapy improves management is unknown and merits prospective evaluation.A poor radiologic response after chemoradiotherapy should prompt complete re-staging, including the abdomen, before surgical salvage.In this patient, pelvic treatment intensification was accompanied by substantial toxicity, and the subsequent failure was peritoneal; the balance of benefit and toxicity of surgery after chemoradiotherapy in GAS should be weighed individually.HER2, MMR/MSI, PD-L1 CPS and, where available, claudin 18.2 should be tested at diagnosis, not at the end of the disease course.Health system barriers that delay multimodal treatment may compound the poor prognosis of this aggressive tumor. ConclusionsGAS should be suspected in postmenopausal women with a deep endocervical mass or a large hydrometra, even when cytology and a first biopsy are negative. Its radioresistance and propensity for peritoneal spread suggest that strategies focused on pelvic treatment alone may be insufficient for some patients, although a single case cannot establish this. Prospective evaluation of staging laparoscopy and comprehensive biomarker testing at diagnosis, together with multicenter registries including patients from Latin America, is needed to guide histology-specific management. full_text: Cervical cancer remains a major public health challenge in Cameroon, where important gaps persist in HPV vaccination, screening, and treatment. This review synthesizes published evidence and programme experience to assess progress in implementing the World Health Organization (WHO) cervical cancer elimination strategy and to identify priorities for national scale-up. We reviewed peer-reviewed literature and publicly available programme and technical documents published between 2015 and 2026, focusing on HPV vaccination, HPV self-sampling, screen–triage–treat approaches, risk-stratified triage, telecytology, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted diagnostics, integration with HIV services, and health-system strengthening. HPV vaccination coverage has improved following adoption of a gender-neutral, single-dose strategy but remains below the WHO target. Cervical cancer screening coverage remains very low, whereas HPV-based screen–triage–treat approaches, self-sampling, thermal ablation, and integration with HIV care platforms show potential to simplify care and reduce loss to follow-up. Extended HPV genotyping and telecytology may improve risk-adapted management and access to specialist expertise, while AI-assisted diagnostics remain investigational and require prospective validation. Major constraints include workforce shortages, fragmented referral pathways, limited diagnostic and treatment capacity, supply-chain weaknesses, and inadequate sustainable financing. Cameroon has generated valuable implementation experience, but the next phase should focus on transitioning from fragmented pilot initiatives to a coordinated national programme supported by strong governance, sustainable financing, digital health infrastructure, and implementation research. DiscussionThis synthesis indicates that cervical cancer elimination in Cameroon is technically feasible but remains constrained primarily by health-system and implementation challenges. Important progress has been made, particularly in HPV vaccination policy and the development of HPV-based screening models; however, population coverage and treatment capacity remain insufficient to meet WHO targets. The persistent gap between innovation and large-scale implementation is therefore the central policy challenge.HPV-based screen–triage–treat strategies, particularly those incorporating self-sampling and same-day treatment, provide a pragmatic approach to reducing loss to follow-up and simplifying the screening cascade. Integration within HIV care platforms may further increase impact by reaching women at elevated risk and leveraging established service-delivery infrastructure.Emerging innovations, including risk-stratified triage, telecytology, and digital health systems, have the potential to improve efficiency and expand access. AI-assisted diagnostics may eventually help address workforce constraints, but their role should remain linked to rigorous prospective validation and appropriate governance.At the same time, persistent workforce shortages, fragmented referral systems, supply-chain constraints, limited treatment capacity, and inadequate financing continue to restrict programme performance. These constraints cannot be addressed by technology alone. Sustainable progress will require coordinated national strategies, stronger governance, investment in human resources, and integration of cervical cancer services across levels of care. National uptake will also depend on whether services are acceptable and accessible to the women and communities they are intended to reach. Evidence from Cameroon supports favourable acceptability of HPV self-sampling and thermal ablation, but national implementation should continue to assess privacy, convenience, information needs, trust, communication of results, and community preferences, particularly among underserved populations (9, 10).The interpretation of these findings has several limitations. This is a narrative synthesis of heterogeneous evidence, including pilot studies, programme reports, and emerging implementation experience, rather than a formal systematic review. Some findings therefore have limited generalizability, and heterogeneity in study designs and implementation settings limits direct comparison across interventions. Important evidence gaps remain regarding cost-effectiveness, long-term outcomes, and the scalability of individual innovations.Overall, the central implementation challenge is to transition from fragmented, pilot-driven initiatives to a coordinated, nationally owned programme. High-impact interventions should be embedded within a strengthened health system rather than implemented as parallel projects. This transition is essential if innovation is to translate into sustained reductions in cervical cancer incidence and mortality. ConclusionCervical cancer elimination in Cameroon is achievable, but progress will depend on coordinated system-level action across the prevention-to-treatment continuum. Scaling HPV vaccination remains the most important primary-prevention priority, and the recent adoption of a single-dose schedule and integration into routine immunization provide opportunities to accelerate coverage (5).Institutionalizing HPV-based screening with self-sampling and risk-adapted triage should be the immediate priority for secondary prevention. Integration within HIV care platforms can improve access for women at particularly high risk, while expansion of diagnostic, surgical, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative-care capacity is essential to ensure that increased detection translates into reduced mortality.Cameroon has generated valuable implementation experience through pilot initiatives in HPV vaccination, screen–triage–treat models, self-sampling, risk stratification, telecytology, and digital health. The next step is to translate these innovations into coordinated national programmes through phased scale-up that matches implementation with health-system capacity and available resources. Sustained political commitment, stronger health-system capacity, long-term financing, effective governance, and implementation research will be essential. Patient and community perspectives, including acceptability, preferences, trust, and barriers to access, should be incorporated into scale-up to ensure that interventions are not only technically effective and feasible but also equitable and sustainable in routine practice (9, 10). IntroductionCervical cancer is a major manifestation of global health inequity, with more than 90% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), despite the availability of highly effective primary and secondary prevention interventions (1). In Cameroon, cervical cancer remains one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers among women, while population-based screening remains limited (2).Persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) is a necessary cause of cervical cancer and provides a clear rationale for primary prevention through vaccination and secondary prevention through early detection and treatment of precancerous lesions. Women living with HIV (WLHIV) are at particularly high risk because impaired immune clearance is associated with increased HPV persistence, more rapid progression to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, and a higher risk of invasive cervical cancer (3, 4).In 2020, the WHO launched its global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer as a public health problem. The strategy established the 90–70–90 targets to be achieved by 2030: 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and 90% of women identified with cervical disease receiving appropriate treatment (1).Achieving these targets requires implementation models adapted to local health-system realities. Workforce shortages, fragmented service delivery, financing constraints, inadequate infrastructure, and weak referral systems can prevent technically effective interventions from achieving population-level impact. Cameroon has introduced a national HPV vaccination programme and has piloted several innovations in HPV-based screening, including self-sampling, risk-stratified triage, same-day treatment, telecytology, and digital follow-up systems. The central challenge is now to move from promising pilot initiatives towards coordinated national implementation.This article provides an integrated national synthesis of cervical cancer prevention and control strategies in Cameroon, linking programme experience with implementation and policy considerations relevant to scale-up in low-resource settings.Approach to evidence synthesisWe conducted a structured narrative synthesis of evidence relevant to implementation of the WHO cervical cancer elimination strategy in Cameroon. The review focused on programme feasibility, acceptability, effectiveness, scalability, and integration within existing health services.Peer-reviewed publications and publicly available programme or technical documents published between 2015 and 2026 were considered. Bibliographic searches of PubMed and Google Scholar used terms related to cervical cancer, HPV, screening, vaccination, HIV, implementation, and Cameroon. Evidence was synthesized thematically to identify implementation barriers, promising service-delivery models, and policy priorities. This approach was not designed as a systematic review or meta-analysis and therefore does not claim comprehensive retrieval of all available evidence.Current status of cervical cancer prevention in CameroonHPV vaccinationCameroon introduced national HPV vaccination in October 2020. Following the introduction of HPV vaccination, coverage initially remained low but improved substantially after the adoption of a gender-neutral, single-dose strategy and intensified community-based delivery. National coverage among girls reached approximately 57% in 2023, while coverage among boys was approximately 26%, remaining below the level required to achieve the WHO elimination target (5).Cameroon has adopted a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule and incorporated HPV vaccination into the routine immunization programme. This policy evolution may facilitate delivery and improve access, particularly in populations with limited contact with health services (5).Nevertheless, several structural and sociobehavioural barriers continue to affect vaccine uptake. These include difficulties reaching out-of-school girls, supply-chain disruptions, limited integration of HPV vaccination into broader adolescent health platforms, and vaccine hesitancy associated with misinformation and low perceived risk. Addressing these barriers will require stronger school- and community-based delivery models, complemented by targeted demand-generation and risk-communication strategies (5).Intersectoral coordination among the Ministries of Health, Education, and Finance is particularly important for sustainable financing, coordinated service delivery, and policy implementation. Monitoring and evaluation systems should also be strengthened. Comprehensive vaccination registries and digital tracking tools can improve measurement of coverage, identify geographic and socioeconomic inequities, and support adaptive programme management. Community engagement and sustained communication will remain essential to strengthening confidence in HPV vaccination.Screening and early treatmentCervical cancer screening coverage in Cameroon remains critically low. In 2018, fewer than 5% of women aged 30–49 years reported having ever been screened (2). Screening services have historically been predominantly opportunistic and cytology-based, with fragmented delivery and limited integration into a coordinated national programme.The Cameroon Baptist Convention Health Services Women’s Health Program is the largest cervical cancer screening initiative in the country and provides an important service-delivery platform in the absence of nationwide programme expansion (6).Several pilot and implementation initiatives have demonstrated the feasibility of simplified HPV-based pathways. In Dschang, Bafoussam, and Yaoundé, the Test–Triage–Treat (3 T) approach has incorporated HPV self-sampling as the primary screening modality, followed by triage using visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology and treatment with thermal ablation when indicated. By reducing the number of visits required, such approaches can limit loss to follow-up and facilitate linkage between screening and treatment (7, 8).HPV self-sampling has shown high acceptability among diverse populations, particularly when embedded within culturally appropriate community-engagement strategies (9). Thermal ablation is also a safe, well-tolerated, and potentially scalable treatment modality that can support a single-visit screen-and-treat approach (10).Decentralization should be considered a core component of national scale-up. HPV testing could be performed at peripheral level 1 and district/intermediate level 2 facilities through decentralized screening units, using the tiered service-delivery infrastructure already being developed for HIV testing and treatment in Cameroon. A similar approach could be considered for HPV-based screening and VIA, while cytology would be better concentrated at facilities with the necessary laboratory infrastructure and trained personnel. Task-shifting to appropriately trained nurses, midwives, and other non-physician providers could further expand access to HPV testing, self-sampling support, VIA, and treatment of eligible precancerous lesions, provided that standardized protocols, competency-based training, quality assurance, supervision, and referral mechanisms are in place.Despite these advances, national scale-up remains constrained by shortages of trained health-care personnel, unequal geographic access to diagnostic and treatment services, and weak referral and follow-up systems (11). Addressing these bottlenecks will require investment in workforce development, decentralization of services, standardized referral pathways, and systems capable of tracking women throughout the screening and treatment cascade.Screening among women living with HIVThe interaction between HIV and HPV is particularly important for cervical cancer prevention in Cameroon. WLHIV have a substantially increased risk of persistent HPV infection, cervical precancer, and cervical cancer (3, 4). This increased risk makes WLHIV a priority population within national cervical cancer prevention strategies.Integrating cervical cancer screening into HIV care platforms offers an important opportunity to improve access and equity by using established service-delivery structures. Such integration can facilitate repeated contact with women at elevated risk and reduce the number of separate visits required to access screening and treatment (12).WHO guidance recommends HPV-based screening for WLHIV from a younger age and at more frequent intervals than in the general population because of their increased risk (13). In Cameroon, differentiated service-delivery models are well established in HIV care, and projects such as OptiTri are exploring how these platforms can be extended to incorporate cervical cancer screening. In these models, HPV testing, including self-sampling, can be integrated into routine antiretroviral therapy services, with triage and treatment organized as close as possible to the point of screening.Emerging programme experience suggests that co-location of cervical cancer screening within HIV services can improve uptake and shorten the interval between testing, diagnosis, and treatment. Integration may also reduce attrition across the screening cascade by using established patient-tracking and follow-up mechanisms (12).Scaling integrated HPV-based screening within HIV services could therefore provide a pragmatic pathway to reach women at particularly high risk. Task-shifting to trained non-physician providers, use of point-of-care technologies, and strengthened referral and follow-up systems could further improve efficiency. However, implementation should be accompanied by reliable procurement and supply chains, clear clinical pathways, and monitoring of cascade indicators such as screening coverage, HPV positivity, treatment uptake, and retention in care.Treatment and care of invasive cervical cancerEffective management of invasive cervical cancer requires standardized, evidence-based national treatment guidelines and a tiered referral system linking community health facilities, district hospitals, and specialized tertiary centres. Such coordination is necessary to ensure timely diagnosis, appropriate staging, treatment initiation, and continuity of care.Strengthening diagnostic capacity is a critical priority. Access to high-quality pathology services, including histopathology and cytology and, where feasible, molecular diagnostics, is fundamental to accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Investments in laboratory infrastructure, quality assurance, equipment, and trained personnel are therefore essential.For early-stage disease, timely surgical management should be expanded. In selected early lesions, conization may be sufficient and can be performed under local anaesthesia using relatively portable equipment, without requiring a full surgical block. More advanced surgical procedures require appropriately equipped operating theatres, trained surgical and anaesthesia teams, blood-transfusion capacity, and postoperative care. Development of gynecologic oncology expertise and standardized surgical protocols is essential to optimize outcomes.For locally advanced and advanced disease, access to multimodal treatment, including radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care, must be strengthened. full_text: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is caused by germline STK11 mutations and increases the risk of gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (GAS). The molecular differences between its precursor, atypical lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia (aLEGH), and invasive GAS are incompletely defined. In this family-based cross-sectional comparison, we used targeted next-generation sequencing and immunohistochemistry to profile a mother with invasive GAS and her daughter with aLEGH, who share the same germline STK11 splice-site variant (c.735-1G>A). Both lesions showed gastric differentiation and loss of detectable STK11 protein expression. No somatic variants were reported for the daughter’s aLEGH sample, whereas the maternal GAS harbored KRAS p. G12C, a truncating ARID1A alteration, FBXW7, and LZTR1 alterations. ARID1A protein expression was lost in the GAS but showed patchy positivity in the aLEGH. These findings identify molecular differences associated with the two observed pathological states and support further investigation of additional somatic alterations in PJS-associated cervical lesions. This family-based cross-sectional comparison provides a hypothesis-generating framework, but does not establish temporal acquisition, clonal relatedness, or causal progression from aLEGH to GAS. Patients and methodsPatients and specimen collectionTwo related individuals: a mother with invasive GAS and her daughter with aLEGH were enrolled under an institutional review board (IRB)-approved protocol after provision of written informed consent. Tissue samples were obtained from diagnostic biopsies and/or hysterectomy material, as applicable. Peripheral blood was collected as the matched germline control. Histopathological diagnoses and IHC findings were reviewed and jointly confirmed by two gynecologic pathologists. HPV testing was negative for high-risk types in both lesions. The mother underwent laparoscopic radical hysterectomy with pelvic adhesiolysis, and the daughter underwent laparoscopic total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy, bilateral ovarian biopsy, and pelvic adhesiolysis. Postoperative surveillance included pelvic ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging at approximately 3 months after surgery, with concurrent measurement of tumor markers and cervical cytology. Specimens were processed for targeted sequencing and immunohistochemistry (IHC) according to the workflow shown in Supplementary Figure S1.Next-generation sequencing and bioinformatic analysisGenomic DNA was extracted from FFPE tumor tissue samples from the maternal GAS and the daughter’s aLEGH, with matched peripheral blood used as the germline control. Targeted NGS was performed using a customized 437-gene panel (GENESEEQPRIME®) at a CAP-accredited laboratory (Nanjing Geneseeq Technology Inc.), with mean sequencing depths of 1000× for tumor and 200× for germline DNA. For the daughter’s aLEGH sample, the reported tumor-cell content was <10% (laboratory reference, ≥10%), and overall sequencing quality control was assessed as “Pass.” The available laboratory report did not provide a sample-specific variant-calling threshold or limit of detection, or gene-level coverage for STK11, KRAS, and ARID1A. The available laboratory reports did not specify whether loss of heterozygosity or loss of the wild-type STK11 allele was assessed. Somatic variants were identified by paired tumor-normal comparison; germline variants were called from blood samples. The germline STK11 c.735-1G>A variant was classified as likely pathogenic in the laboratory report. Copy number alterations and clonal hematopoiesis-related variants were filtered using standard algorithms. All candidate mutations were manually reviewed, with full bioinformatic parameters detailed in the Supplementary Methods.ImmunohistochemistryIHC was performed for gastric markers (MUC6, MUC5AC, Claudin18.2), cell cycle and hormone markers (p16, ER, PR, Ki-67), CDX-2, STK11, ARID1A, CD8, and PD-L1 using standard protocols. STK11 and ARID1A IHC were performed in this study; findings for the other markers were obtained from the original pathology reports. Normal cervical tissue was used as a positive control for STK11 staining. Positivity criteria were applied as follows: nuclear loss of STK11 or ARID1A; membranous PD-L1 in ≥1% of tumor cells; and semiquantitative assessment of CD8+ intratumoral and stromal infiltration. The histopathological diagnoses and IHC findings were reviewed and jointly confirmed by two gynecologic pathologists. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis family-based cross-sectional comparison examines stage-associated molecular differences between aLEGH and invasive GAS in the setting of a shared germline STK11 splice-site variant (Jiang et al., 2026; Yoshida et al., 2026). The comparison involves a PJS-affected mother with invasive GAS and her daughter with aLEGH, who share the same germline STK11 splice-site variant. The daughter’s aLEGH had no somatic variants reported in the available laboratory report. Given the tumor-cell content of <10% and the limitations of the available report, this result should be interpreted cautiously and does not exclude low-frequency variants, alterations outside the panel, or genomic events not reliably captured by the assay. By contrast, the mother’s GAS harbored somatic alterations: KRAS p. G12C and truncating ARID1A mutations (Park et al., 2021; Kuruma et al., 2026), alongside FBXW7 and LZTR1 alterations (Fan et al., 2022; Ko et al., 2023). The complete loss of ARID1A protein in the mother’s GAS, compared with the patchy positivity retained in the daughter’s aLEGH, is consistent with an association between the ARID1A alteration and the invasive lesion. However, this comparison does not establish temporal acquisition or causality (Bitler et al., 2015). These observations are compatible with, but do not prove, an association between additional somatic alterations and invasive disease in PJS-associated cervical gastric-type lesions (Kuruma et al., 2026; Shackelford and Shaw, 2009).The molecular findings identified in the mother’s GAS are exploratory and do not establish therapeutic or predictive relevance. The KRAS p. G12C mutation introduces a cysteine residue that creates a unique covalent-binding pocket, rendering this variant pharmacologically tractable with approved inhibitors in lung cancer (Warnecke and Nagasaka, 2024; Skoulidis et al., 2021). However, its therapeutic relevance in GAS remains unestablished. The original pathology reports described Claudin18.2 staining as partially positive in both lesions but did not specify the percentage of positive tumor cells, staining intensity, or scoring method. Claudin18.2 has been described as a potential therapeutic target in GAS (Yang et al., 2024). In the context of gastric cancer, higher thresholds (e.g., ≥75% tumor cells with moderate-to-strong staining) have been used for patient selection in clinical trials and regulatory approvals (Shah et al., 2023; Shitara et al., 2023). However, this threshold has not been validated for cervical GAS. Because the available pathology reports provide only a qualitative description of partial positivity, these findings cannot establish eligibility for Claudin18.2-directed treatment and should be considered exploratory. Similarly, ARID1A loss has been associated with synthetic-lethal vulnerabilities to EZH2 and PARP inhibition in preclinical and early-phase studies (Bitler et al., 2015; Hein et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2015). These case-level findings should not guide treatment selection and require confirmation in larger PJS-associated GAS series.The immune profile was noninflamed in both samples, with no identified CD8+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and negative tumor-cell PD-L1 staining, and no discernible difference between the two lesions (Figure 2). HPV E6 splicing-associated immune networks have been investigated in HPV-related cervical cancer (Jiang et al., 2022). However, these findings cannot be assumed to apply to PJS-associated, HPV-independent GAS or aLEGH. The CD8 and PD-L1 findings in the present cases are descriptive and do not establish an immune mechanism in these lesions. Treatment decisions in recurrent or metastatic disease should integrate validated PD-L1 scoring, mismatch-repair and microsatellite-instability status, tumor mutational burden when appropriate, prior treatment, and the totality of clinical evidence (Abu-Rustum et al., 2025). The predictive role of STK11 alteration in GAS specifically remains undefined (Skoulidis et al., 2018; Colombo et al., 2021).We acknowledge the inherent limitation of a two-patient, single-family, cross-sectional study, which precludes formal statistical generalization and cannot distinguish stage-associated differences from patient-specific, age-related, or other unmeasured sources of heterogeneity. The available pathology records did not specify the extent of sampling of the daughter’s 4.8-cm lesion; therefore, complete sampling cannot be confirmed. The rarity of this comparison provides a hypothesis-generating observation of molecular differences between aLEGH and invasive GAS, but does not establish a progression sequence or a causal role for any individual alteration. The residual aLEGH at the periphery of the maternal tumor was not separately microdissected or sequenced; therefore, its molecular relationship to the invasive GAS could not be assessed. Normal cervical tissue was used as a positive control for STK11 IHC. The absence of detectable STK11 staining in the lesions does not establish loss of heterozygosity, copy-number loss, or a somatic second hit. Our findings are broadly consistent with prior cross-sectional genomic studies in GAS (Park et al., 2021; Kuruma et al., 2026). Future functional validation using cervical organoid models or genetically engineered mouse systems is warranted to formally test the role of KRAS, ARID1A, FBXW7, and LZTR1 alterations in cervical epithelial transformation (Fan et al., 2022; Ko et al., 2023). Prospective studies with longitudinal sampling will be needed to clarify the natural history of PJS-associated aLEGH and inform surveillance strategies (Jiang et al., 2024; Ishiguro et al., 2025). The integrated workflow established here (Supplementary Figure S1) may serve as a framework for future investigations.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn this family-based cross-sectional comparison, invasive GAS showed a more complex somatic profile than aLEGH despite shared germline STK11 splice-site variation and gastric differentiation. The findings showed that additional alterations, including KRAS and ARID1A events, were observed in the invasive GAS; however, the comparison does not establish temporal acquisition, clonal relatedness, or causality. These observations are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger longitudinal, microdissection-based, and functional studies before they can inform surveillance or treatment strategies.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionGastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (GAS) is one of the deadliest gynecologic malignancies. Unlike conventional cervical cancers, which are largely preventable and chemoradiation-responsive, it presents at advanced stages, resists standard therapy, and carries a median overall survival of only 26 months (Gordhandas et al., 2022; Nishio et al., 2019). Its resistance is rooted in a distinct molecular identity, closer to gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas than to human papillomavirus-driven cervical carcinomas (Park et al., 2021). For patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), a hereditary disorder caused by germline STK11 mutations, this risk is magnified: GAS is a well-recognized, yet poorly understood, component of their malignancy spectrum.The precursor lesion, atypical lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia (aLEGH), is a morphologically distinct gastric metaplastic lesion and is considered a direct neoplastic forerunner of GAS (Miyamoto et al., 2022). However, the natural history of PJS-associated aLEGH, particularly its molecular relationship to GAS, remains incompletely defined. A recent cohort study reported that PJS-associated aLEGH presents at a younger age than sporadic cases and may undergo malignant transformation over a short interval in some patients (Jiang et al., 2026). Cross-sectional genomic studies have described STK11 alterations and additional genomic changes in GAS (Kuruma et al., 2026). These findings raise questions about molecular differences associated with invasive disease but do not establish the timing or causal role of individual alterations. The implications for surveillance and treatment selection remain uncertain. STK11 is a well-established tumor suppressor, although the relationship between STK11 dysfunction and epithelial tumor progression remains incompletely understood (Shackelford and Shaw, 2009; Jiang et al., 2025). Individual reports have documented the co-occurrence of PJS and GAS (Li et al., 2026).Here, we report a family-based cross-sectional comparison of a PJS-affected mother with invasive GAS and her daughter with aLEGH, who share the same germline STK11 splice-site variant. Previous studies have described PJS-associated cervical lesions (Gordhandas et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026) and additional somatic alterations in established GAS (Park et al., 2021; Kuruma et al., 2026; Yoshida et al., 2026). However, the molecular differences between PJS-associated aLEGH and invasive GAS remain incompletely defined. Our aim was to determine whether stage-associated molecular differences were detectable between these two pathological states using integrated targeted sequencing and immunohistochemistry. Because the lesions were obtained from different individuals at different ages, this study is hypothesis-generating and does not establish a progression sequence. Next-generation sequencing and bioinformatic analysisGenomic DNA was extracted from FFPE tumor tissue samples from the maternal GAS and the daughter’s aLEGH, with matched peripheral blood used as the germline control. Targeted NGS was performed using a customized 437-gene panel (GENESEEQPRIME®) at a CAP-accredited laboratory (Nanjing Geneseeq Technology Inc.), with mean sequencing depths of 1000× for tumor and 200× for germline DNA. For the daughter’s aLEGH sample, the reported tumor-cell content was <10% (laboratory reference, ≥10%), and overall sequencing quality control was assessed as “Pass.” The available laboratory report did not provide a sample-specific variant-calling threshold or limit of detection, or gene-level coverage for STK11, KRAS, and ARID1A. The available laboratory reports did not specify whether loss of heterozygosity or loss of the wild-type STK11 allele was assessed. Somatic variants were identified by paired tumor-normal comparison; germline variants were called from blood samples. The germline STK11 c.735-1G>A variant was classified as likely pathogenic in the laboratory report. Copy number alterations and clonal hematopoiesis-related variants were filtered using standard algorithms. All candidate mutations were manually reviewed, with full bioinformatic parameters detailed in the Supplementary Methods. ImmunohistochemistryIHC was performed for gastric markers (MUC6, MUC5AC, Claudin18.2), cell cycle and hormone markers (p16, ER, PR, Ki-67), CDX-2, STK11, ARID1A, CD8, and PD-L1 using standard protocols. STK11 and ARID1A IHC were performed in this study; findings for the other markers were obtained from the original pathology reports. Normal cervical tissue was used as a positive control for STK11 staining. Positivity criteria were applied as follows: nuclear loss of STK11 or ARID1A; membranous PD-L1 in ≥1% of tumor cells; and semiquantitative assessment of CD8+ intratumoral and stromal infiltration. The histopathological diagnoses and IHC findings were reviewed and jointly confirmed by two gynecologic pathologists. Shared germline predisposition and divergent phenotypesThe mother (43 years) presented with FIGO 2018 stage IB3 well-differentiated GAS (3.9 × 4.2 × 4.7 cm on MRI), whereas the daughter (22 years) was diagnosed with aLEGH manifesting as a 4.8-cm lesion on CT (MRI was contraindicated due to surgical clips) (Figure 1). Both patients had carried a PJS diagnosis since childhood (mother at age 6, daughter at age 14) and had histories of intestinal obstruction or intussusception requiring surgical intervention (Table 1). The mother also harbored a classic PJS-associated ovarian sex cord tumor with annular tubules (SCTAT). The mother underwent laparoscopic radical hysterectomy with pelvic adhesiolysis, and the daughter underwent laparoscopic total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy, bilateral ovarian biopsy, and pelvic adhesiolysis. full_text: AbstractObjectiveTo evaluate the association between JAM3/PAX1 methylation and cervical lesion severity and assess its diagnostic performance, alone and in combination with HPV16/18 genotyping, for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN2+) in hrHPV-positive women.MethodsA total of 205 treatment-negative hrHPV-positive women with available JAM3/PAX1 methylation results and histopathological diagnoses were included in this hospital-based study. The association between methylation positivity and cervical lesion severity was evaluated using the Cochran–Armitage trend test. A subset of 105 participants with complete HPV genotyping, cytology, methylation, and histopathological data was further analyzed using ordinal logistic regression and diagnostic performance measures, including sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).ResultsAmong the 205 participants, JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity increased with cervical lesion severity, with positivity rates of 20.00% in the normal group, 23.53% in CIN1, 33.33% in CIN2, 61.43% in CIN3, and 65.12% in cervical cancer (P for trend < 0.001). In the complete-data subset (n = 105), JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity (OR = 5.02, 95% CI: 2.15–11.77) and HPV16/18 positivity (OR = 3.88, 95% CI: 1.75–8.60) were independently associated with higher cervical lesion grades. Parallel testing of JAM3/PAX1 methylation and HPV16/18 genotyping achieved a sensitivity of 86.81% and a specificity of 50.00% for CIN2+ detection, whereas sequential testing yielded a sensitivity of 43.96% and a specificity of 92.86%.ConclusionJAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity was associated with cervical lesion severity in hrHPV-positive women. Combining JAM3/PAX1 methylation with HPV16/18 genotyping provided different sensitivity–specificity trade-offs for CIN2+ detection. These findings suggest that JAM3/PAX1 methylation may serve as an adjunctive marker for cervical lesion risk assessment, although further validation in larger and less-selected screening populations is needed.Keywords: cervical lesions, CIN2+, DNA methylation, high-risk human papillomavirus, JAM3/PAX1, risk stratification 2.Materials and methods2.1.General informationThis hospital-based study initially assessed 325 women who underwent JAM3/PAX1 methylation testing at the Gynecologic Oncology Center of the Affiliated Cancer Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University between September 2024 and December 2025. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) women aged ≥25 years with a history of sexual activity; (2) confirmed baseline hrHPV positivity; (3) availability of JAM3/PAX1 methylation results obtained before treatment; and (4) definitive histopathological diagnosis. The exclusion criteria were: (1) absence of definitive histopathological diagnosis; (2) history of hysterectomy; and (3) previous treatment for cervical cancer before methylation testing, including surgery or chemoradiotherapy.Among these women, 19 were excluded due to the absence of definitive histopathological diagnoses, and 4 were excluded because of a history of hysterectomy. An additional 97 patients who underwent methylation testing after treatment for cervical cancer were excluded, as the present study focused on cervical lesion assessment before treatment. Finally, 205 treatment-negative women with confirmed baseline hrHPV positivity and definitive histopathological diagnoses were included in the analysis (Figure 1).Figure 1Participant selection and analytic samples.Flowchart showing study cohort selection: Three hundred twenty-five women were initially assessed for JAM3/PAX1 methylation. One hundred twenty were excluded due to no definitive histopathology (nineteen), history of hysterectomy (four), or previous cervical cancer treatment (ninety-seven). The final eligible cohort had 205 women with confirmed baseline high-risk HPV positivity and definitive histopathological diagnosis. All 205 were used for the primary analysis of JAM3/PAX1 methylation and cervical lesion severity, with 5 normal, 51 CIN1, 36 CIN2, 70 CIN3, and 43 cancer cases. One hundred five formed a complete-data subset for HPV genotyping, LBC, methylation, and pathology for further analysis.According to histopathological findings, the 205 participants were classified into five groups: normal (n = 5), CIN1 (n = 51), CIN2 (n = 36), CIN3 (n = 70), and cervical cancer (n = 43). Clinical and laboratory data, including age, hrHPV testing results, available HPV genotyping and LBC results, JAM3/PAX1 methylation status, histopathological findings, and treatment history, were collected.Among the 205 participants, 105 had complete HPV genotyping, LBC, JAM3/PAX1 methylation, and histopathological data and were included in the ordinal logistic regression and diagnostic performance analyses. The overall association between JAM3/PAX1 methylation status and cervical lesion severity was evaluated in all 205 participants.2.2.Laboratory detection methods2.2.1.HPV testingHPV detection and genotyping were performed using a commercial human papillomavirus nucleic acid detection kit (Ningbo Haier Gene Co., Ltd., China). This method, through PCR amplification and capillary electrophoresis fragment analysis, can detect 25 HPV types (6, 11, 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 42, 43, 44, 45, 51, 52, 53, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68, 73, 81, 82, 83). In this study, 14 hrHPV types (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68) were identified. Detection of any high-risk HPV genotype was considered indicative of hrHPV positivity.2.2.2.Liquid-based cytologyLiquid-based cytology (LBC) was performed using the BD SurePathTM liquid-based cytology system (Becton, Dickinson and Company, USA), and experienced cytologists interpreted the slides in a blinded manner according to the 2014 Bethesda System (TBS) classification criteria (11). Result judgment: NILM (Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy) is a negative LBC result; ASC-US (Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance), AGC (Atypical glandular cells), LSIL (Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), ASC-H (Atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), HSIL (High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), SCC (Squamous cell carcinoma), AIS (Adenocarcinoma in situ), ADC (Adenocarcinoma) are all positive results of LBC.2.2.3.Methylation detectionThe Human PAX1/JAM3 Gene Methylation Detection Kit (OriginPoly Bio-Tec Co., Ltd., Beijing, China) was used to assess DNA methylation status in cervical exfoliated cells. Genomic DNA was extracted from cervical exfoliated cell samples, and DNA concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Following bisulfite conversion, the methylation status of PAX1 and JAM3 was determined using multiplex real-time PCR with fluorescence probes according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The PCR cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation at 96 °C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 15 s, annealing at 64 °C for 5 s, and extension at 60 °C for 30 s (fluorescence acquisition). GAPDH was used as the internal reference gene. Methylation positivity was defined as ΔCt (PAX1) ≤ 6.6 or ΔCt (JAM3) ≤ 10.0, with positivity for either gene considered a positive JAM3/PAX1 methylation result.2.3.Colposcopy and pathological diagnosisColposcopic examinations were performed by experienced gynecologic oncologists from tertiary oncology hospitals. Categorical variables presented as numbers and percentages. Participants were stratified into four age groups (<40, 40–49, 50–59, and ≥60 years) for age-related analyses. Pearson’s chi-square test was used to assess differences in histopathological grade distributions and JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity across age groups. The Cochran–Armitage trend test was used to evaluate the trends in JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity across cervical lesion grades and age groups, as well as trends in HPV16/18 positivity across cervical lesion grades. Ordinal logistic regression was performed in the subset of 105 participants with complete HPV genotyping, LBC, JAM3/PAX1 methylation, and histopathological data to assess the associations of JAM3/PAX1 methylation status, HPV16/18 positivity, and LBC results with cervical lesion severity. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.Diagnostic performance for detecting CIN2+ was evaluated in the same subset by calculating sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Parallel testing was defined as a positive result for either JAM3/PAX1 methylation or HPV16/18 genotyping, whereas sequential testing required positivity for both. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectiveTo evaluate the association between JAM3/PAX1 methylation and cervical lesion severity and assess its diagnostic performance, alone and in combination with HPV16/18 genotyping, for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN2+) in hrHPV-positive women.MethodsA total of 205 treatment-negative hrHPV-positive women with available JAM3/PAX1 methylation results and histopathological diagnoses were included in this hospital-based study. The association between methylation positivity and cervical lesion severity was evaluated using the Cochran–Armitage trend test. A subset of 105 participants with complete HPV genotyping, cytology, methylation, and histopathological data was further analyzed using ordinal logistic regression and diagnostic performance measures, including sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).ResultsAmong the 205 participants, JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity increased with cervical lesion severity, with positivity rates of 20.00% in the normal group, 23.53% in CIN1, 33.33% in CIN2, 61.43% in CIN3, and 65.12% in cervical cancer (P for trend < 0.001). In the complete-data subset (n = 105), JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity (OR = 5.02, 95% CI: 2.15–11.77) and HPV16/18 positivity (OR = 3.88, 95% CI: 1.75–8.60) were independently associated with higher cervical lesion grades. Parallel testing of JAM3/PAX1 methylation and HPV16/18 genotyping achieved a sensitivity of 86.81% and a specificity of 50.00% for CIN2+ detection, whereas sequential testing yielded a sensitivity of 43.96% and a specificity of 92.86%.ConclusionJAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity was associated with cervical lesion severity in hrHPV-positive women. Combining JAM3/PAX1 methylation with HPV16/18 genotyping provided different sensitivity–specificity trade-offs for CIN2+ detection. These findings suggest that JAM3/PAX1 methylation may serve as an adjunctive marker for cervical lesion risk assessment, although further validation in larger and less-selected screening populations is needed.Keywords: cervical lesions, CIN2+, DNA methylation, high-risk human papillomavirus, JAM3/PAX1, risk stratification
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Materials and methods2.1.General informationThis hospital-based study initially assessed 325 women who underwent JAM3/PAX1 methylation testing at the Gynecologic Oncology Center of the Affiliated Cancer Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University between September 2024 and December 2025. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) women aged ≥25 years with a history of sexual activity; (2) confirmed baseline hrHPV positivity; (3) availability of JAM3/PAX1 methylation results obtained before treatment; and (4) definitive histopathological diagnosis. An additional 97 patients who underwent methylation testing after treatment for cervical cancer were excluded, as the present study focused on cervical lesion assessment before treatment. Finally, 205 treatment-negative women with confirmed baseline hrHPV positivity and definitive histopathological diagnoses were included in the analysis (Figure 1).Figure 1Participant selection and analytic samples.Flowchart showing study cohort selection: Three hundred twenty-five women were initially assessed for JAM3/PAX1 methylation. One hundred twenty were excluded due to no definitive histopathology (nineteen), history of hysterectomy (four), or previous cervical cancer treatment (ninety-seven). All 205 were used for the primary analysis of JAM3/PAX1 methylation and cervical lesion severity, with 5 normal, 51 CIN1, 36 CIN2, 70 CIN3, and 43 cancer cases. Clinical and laboratory data, including age, hrHPV testing results, available HPV genotyping and LBC results, JAM3/PAX1 methylation status, histopathological findings, and treatment history, were collected.Among the 205 participants, 105 had complete HPV genotyping, LBC, JAM3/PAX1 methylation, and histopathological data and were included in the ordinal logistic regression and diagnostic performance analyses. The overall association between JAM3/PAX1 methylation status and cervical lesion severity was evaluated in all 205 participants.2.2.Laboratory detection methods2.2.1.HPV testingHPV detection and genotyping were performed using a commercial human papillomavirus nucleic acid detection kit (Ningbo Haier Gene Co., Ltd., China). This method, through PCR amplification and capillary electrophoresis fragment analysis, can detect 25 HPV types (6, 11, 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 42, 43, 44, 45, 51, 52, 53, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68, 73, 81, 82, 83). In this study, 14 hrHPV types (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68) were identified. The PCR cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation at 96 °C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 15 s, annealing at 64 °C for 5 s, and extension at 60 °C for 30 s (fluorescence acquisition). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis hospital-based study evaluated the association between JAM3/PAX1 methylation and cervical lesion severity in 205 treatment-negative hrHPV-positive women and further assessed its diagnostic performance, alone and in combination with HPV16/18 genotyping, in a subset of 105 participants with complete diagnostic data. Consistent with previous studies, DNA methylation has shown potential as a molecular biomarker for identifying high-grade cervical lesions (13–18). Our findings provide additional evidence for the potential application of JAM3/PAX1 methylation in cervical lesion risk assessment among hrHPV-positive women.Ordinal logistic regression analysis showed that JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity (OR = 5.02, 95% CI: 2.15–11.77, P < 0.001) and HPV16/18 positivity (OR = 3.88, 95% CI: 1.75–8.60, P < 0.001) were independently associated with higher cervical lesion grades after adjustment for the other test variables included in the model, whereas LBC positivity was not significantly associated with lesion severity (P = 0.912). The Cochran–Armitage trend test demonstrated that JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity increased with cervical lesion severity (χ2 for trend = 24.51, P < 0.001), from 20.00% in women with normal histopathology to 65.12% in those with cervical cancer. These findings suggest that JAM3/PAX1 methylation status may reflect the severity of existing cervical lesions. However, this cross-sectional association does not establish its ability to predict subsequent lesion progression.Regarding diagnostic performance for CIN2+ detection, HPV16/18 genotyping alone achieved an AUC of 0.692, while JAM3/PAX1 methylation alone achieved an AUC of 0.676. Parallel testing combining HPV16/18 genotyping and JAM3/PAX1 methylation increased sensitivity to 86.81%, but specificity decreased to 50.00%, with a test-positive proportion of 81.90%. In contrast, sequential testing requiring positivity for both markers achieved a specificity of 92.86% and a PPV of 97.56%, but sensitivity decreased to 43.96%, with a test-positive proportion of 39.05%. Both combined strategies yielded an AUC of 0.684, which did not exceed that of HPV16/18 genotyping alone. These results indicate different sensitivity–specificity trade-offs between parallel and sequential testing strategies rather than superior overall diagnostic performance. Further studies are needed to determine whether these combinations could improve clinical triage decisions or reduce unnecessary colposcopy referrals.This study has several limitations. First, the study was conducted at a single tertiary oncology hospital with a clinically enriched population, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to general screening populations. Second, the diagnostic performance analysis was based on only 105 participants with complete data, including 91 CIN2+ cases and only 14 participants with lesions below CIN2. This highly selected sample composition may affect the precision and generalizability of specificity and predictive value estimates, particularly the high PPV observed in sequential testing. Third, the ordinal logistic regression model included only JAM3/PAX1 methylation, HPV16/18 positivity, and LBC results, and residual confounding from other factors, including age, cannot be excluded. Finally, this study evaluated existing cervical lesions without longitudinal clinical outcomes; therefore, the predictive value of JAM3/PAX1 methylation for future lesion progression could not be assessed. Larger, multicenter prospective studies involving more representative hrHPV-positive populations are needed to validate these findings and clarify their potential clinical utility.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsIn conclusion, JAM3/PAX1 methylation positivity was significantly associated with higher cervical lesion grades in hrHPV-positive women. Combining JAM3/PAX1 methylation with HPV16/18 genotyping provided different sensitivity–specificity trade-offs for CIN2+ detection, although neither combined strategy yielded a higher AUC than HPV16/18 genotyping alone. These findings suggest that JAM3/PAX1 methylation may serve as an adjunctive marker for cervical lesion risk assessment in hospital-based populations. Further validation in larger and more representative cohorts is warranted.
